## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can a machine pass its normal operating tests and still fail when its protective response is needed?_

A mobile manipulator can complete an aisle run while leaving its stopping mechanism untested. A stalled proposer, an old observation, or a loss of power challenges a different claim from successful task completion: the machine must contain motion while the fault is active. Establishing that claim requires deliberate disturbances, physical measurements independent of the failing component, and acceptance conditions fixed before the test. Missing observations and untested conditions limit what the result can support. Verification makes those limits explicit before release grants authority for an action to cross the causal boundary.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Derive test conditions and stopping oracles from the machine's operating envelope
- Derive faults from design assumptions, physical hazards, and authority-transfer failures
- Select qualification environments that exercise the causal mechanism behind each claim
- Interpret temporal safety margins and search for disturbances that violate them
- Evaluate the assumptions limiting simulation transfer, rare-event estimates, and formal proofs
- Design hardware injections with independent witnesses and precommitted acceptance conditions
- Assemble fault records that preserve failed, invalid, unobservable, and untested cases

:::

## The Claim a Fault Trial Must Test {#sec-verification-fault-injection}

A proposer can stop renewing commands while the base continues toward the rack end. The authority record specifies who should take over, but that specification does not show that the permission path survives the fault or that the brakes respond in time. Integrated verification deliberately creates the failure and measures the response through to physical motion.

Policy evaluation in @sec-evaluation asks how well a learned candidate performs under declared tasks and conditions. Here the object under test is the assembled machine: proposer, permission path, communication, power, and body. A strong evaluation result does not establish that an independent stop still works when the proposer stalls. Conversely, a successful protective stop does not show that the policy completes its task well. Release needs both kinds of evidence for the same configuration. It also distinguishes proposer autonomy from whole-machine task success: a permitted least-change correction can preserve successful service while exposing a limitation of the raw proposal.

The **digital twin delusion**\index{Digital twin delusion!simulation limits} treats passing simulated assertions as sufficient evidence for physical safety. A simulator can represent timing, electrical, and contact effects only to the extent that its models include and validate them. An omitted power fault cannot fail a simulated controller. Operational logs invite the corresponding mistake. Incident-free exposure, however long, leaves unencountered faults untested.

**Adversarial fault injection** turns a claim into a deliberate disturbance under independent physical containment. The engineering sequence begins with the conditions in which the claim should hold, derives faults that challenge its premises, and chooses a test environment that exercises the relevant mechanism. A precommitted oracle then scores the measured response, and the resulting fault record preserves both the evidence and its limits.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_as.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Act-to-Sense feedback edge."}

*The Act $\to$ Sense feedback loop: physical verification closes the causal loop from actuator response back to sensor observation under active fault injection.*
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-rack-end-oracle
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RACK-END FAULT-INJECTION ORACLE FOR THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: fault-injection scene, operating envelope, fault list, oracles,
# │          hardware injection, fault manifest, fallacies, and summary.
# │ Goal: Derive the two oracle bounds (powered deceleration onset after the last valid renewal,
# │       stopping distance at the aisle speed) and the envelope points that
# │       F1-F4 and A1-A4 are injected at, all from the machine's registry entry.
# │ Show: 82 ms onset bound; 969.0 mm budget and 131.0 mm spare at 1.3 m/s;
# │       100.8 ms of travel in that spare, 663.3 ms at the 0.8 m/s takeover
# │       speed; the 1.44 m/s dry and 1.23 m/s inspected-floor ceilings; the
# │       37.8 V sustained drive-bus sag, 4.8 V above the 33 V converter
# │       lockout (150 A to cross it); the permission rail's 2.0 s hold-up against
# │       1313.43 ms from flag to brakes set (F4b); F1's stop oracle from the
# │       last valid renewal (751.9 mm at 1.3 m/s); the F1 record's oracle at
# │       the restricted 1.0 m/s point (629.6 mm from the last valid renewal);
# │       the Class 3 tank contrast (volume, not distance); F2's refusal
# │       threshold, the 51.6 ms budgeted dispatch age plus the 0.2 ms clock-conversion
# │       bound (51.8 ms upper age); the unbudgeted queue length that exhausts
# │       the spare (100.8 ms, about three-quarters of the pre-brake subtotal);
# │       a late-onset F1 trace's signed and normalized margins; the SoC's share
# │       of the bus transient (1.6 A of 70 A); the discrepancy a spare-sized
# │       simulated margin tolerates (0.131 in a 1 m position norm).
# │ How: the jerk-limited S-curve stop (calc_scurve_stop_distance / _time,
# │      calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity) with the jerk bound taken as the
# │      reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit, as in
# │      @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix, and the three fixed overheads;
# │      calc_voltage_droop for the 48 V drive bus (M6); tank arithmetic by
# │      conservation of volume.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, kilogram, microsecond, millisecond, second, meter, millimeter
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_scurve_stop_distance,
    calc_scurve_stop_time,
    calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity,
)
from mlsysim.physics import calc_voltage_droop
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_time,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_voltage,
    fmt_current,
    fmt_temperature,
    fmt_mass,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_power,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class RackEndVerification:
    """Oracle bounds and envelope points for fault injection at the rack end."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived
    eps_sync = 0.2 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (clock-conversion bound, @sec-perception-observation-contract)
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    heartbeat_timeout = AISLE.heartbeat_timeout  # category: chosen
    enforcer_deadline = AISLE.enforcer_deadline  # category: chosen
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    t_takeover = AISLE.t_takeover_in_loop  # category: illustrative
    v_takeover = AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop  # category: chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    eps_track = AISLE.eps_track  # category: illustrative
    side_clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative
    mu_dry = AISLE.mu_dry  # category: illustrative
    mu_insp = AISLE.mu_inspected_floor  # category: illustrative
    payload = RM.onboard_payload_capacity  # category: chosen
    bus_nominal = RM.drive_bus_nominal  # category: datasheet (48 V-class pack, nominal)
    bus_low = RM.drive_bus_battery_low  # category: datasheet (pack minimum)
    bus_r = RM.drive_bus_resistance  # category: illustrative (source path; needs a measured value)
    bus_uvlo = RM.drive_bus_uvlo  # category: datasheet (converter input lockout)
    i_rail = AISLE.i_rail_transient  # category: illustrative
    rail_holdup = RM.permission_rail_holdup  # category: chosen
    brake_engage_max = RM.spring_brake_engage_max  # category: illustrative
    g = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # physical constant (defined); category: derived
    # Scenario assumptions local to this chapter
    ambient_lo = ureg.Quantity(5.0, ureg.degC)  # scenario assumption; category: chosen
    ambient_hi = ureg.Quantity(35.0, ureg.degC)  # scenario assumption; category: chosen
    lease_probe = 5 * millisecond  # proposal injected after expiry; scenario assumption; category: chosen
    v_restricted = (
        1.0 * meter / second
    )  # restricted-mode aisle speed on inspected floors, below the inspected-floor ceiling; scenario assumption; category: chosen
    late_onset = 30 * millisecond  # example late powered deceleration onset (STL margin); scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    soc_power = RM.brain_soc.tdp_max  # category: datasheet (application SoC maximum module power)
    converter_eff = RM.drive_bus_converter_efficiency  # category: datasheet (typical converter efficiency)
    drive_current_limit = RM.drive_current_limit  # category: chosen (per-motor datasheet peak)
    drive_wheels = RM.drive_wheel_count  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    overhead = (delta_loc + delta_margin + eps_track).to(millimeter)
    # Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_drive, a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
    onset_bound = (t_lease + t_tick + t_bus + t_act).to(millisecond)
    upper_age = (t_age + eps_sync).to(millisecond)  # F2: dispatch-only upper-age threshold; admission/execution age continues
    lease_probe_at = (t_lease + lease_probe).to(millisecond)
    chunk_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    c2_distance = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter)
    budget = (v_aisle * tau_delay + c2_distance + overhead).to(millimeter)
    spare = (d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
    t_spare = (spare / v_aisle).to(millisecond)
    per_ms = (v_aisle * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)
    budget_takeover = (v_takeover * tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_takeover, a_brake, j_brake) + overhead).to(millimeter)
    spare_takeover = (d_clear - budget_takeover).to(millimeter)
    t_spare_takeover = (spare_takeover / v_takeover).to(millisecond)
    ceiling_dry = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay, a_brake, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)
    mu_min = float((a_brake / g).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    # The floor caps the deceleration; the jerk bound belongs to the load and is unchanged.
    a_insp = min(a_brake, (mu_insp * g).to(meter / second**2))
    budget_insp = (v_aisle * tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_insp, j_brake) + overhead).to(millimeter)
    ceiling_insp = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay, a_insp, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)
    bus_sag = calc_voltage_droop(i_rail, bus_r).to(ureg.volt)
    bus_min = (bus_low - bus_sag).to(ureg.volt)  # sustained screen from the depleted pack
    bus_margin = (bus_min - bus_uvlo).to(ureg.volt)
    i_cross = ((bus_low - bus_uvlo) / bus_r).to(ureg.ampere)  # step that would reach the lockout
    # F4: from the undervoltage or feed-loss flag, stop onset, the longest resident
    # stop inside the envelope (inspected floor at its ceiling), and brakes set
    flag_onset = (t_tick + t_bus + t_act).to(millisecond)
    stop_insp_ceiling = calc_scurve_stop_time(ceiling_insp, a_insp, j_brake).to(millisecond)
    flag_to_set = (flag_onset + stop_insp_ceiling + brake_engage_max).to(millisecond)
    holdup_margin = (rail_holdup - flag_to_set).to(millisecond)
    # F1 record at the restricted point, scored from the last valid renewal
    f1_preonset = (v_restricted * onset_bound).to(millimeter)
    f1_c2 = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_restricted, a_insp, j_brake).to(millimeter)
    f1_stop_bound = (f1_preonset + f1_c2 + eps_track).to(millimeter)
    # F1 at the aisle speed, scored from the same event (last valid renewal)
    f1_aisle_stop_bound = (v_aisle * onset_bound + c2_distance + eps_track).to(millimeter)
    budget_restricted = (v_restricted * tau_delay + f1_c2 + overhead).to(millimeter)
    late_extra = (v_aisle * late_onset).to(millimeter)
    # Signed margins of one late-onset F1 trace against the renewal-referenced oracle
    onset_late = (onset_bound + late_onset).to(millisecond)
    travel_late = (f1_aisle_stop_bound + late_extra).to(millimeter)
    rho_onset = (onset_bound - onset_late).to(millisecond)
    rho_dist = (f1_aisle_stop_bound - travel_late).to(millimeter)
    # Normalized by chosen scales equal to the bounds themselves
    rho_onset_n = float((rho_onset / onset_bound).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    rho_dist_n = float((rho_dist / f1_aisle_stop_bound).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    # Shared-bus sag attribution: the application SoC's maximum draw from the depleted bus
    soc_current = (soc_power / (bus_low * converter_eff)).to(ureg.ampere)
    drive_peak = (drive_current_limit * drive_wheels).to(ureg.ampere)
    soc_share = float((soc_current / i_rail).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    # Sim-to-real instance: position error in meters (L_phi = 1 m per unit of the norm);
    # a simulated margin equal to the spare tolerates at most this discrepancy
    eps_gap_max = float((spare / (1 * meter)).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    # Fallacy: an unbudgeted queue spends the spare at v per unit time, so the
    # queue length that exhausts it is the spare's travel time t_spare.
    queue_exhaust_ratio = (t_spare / tau_delay).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(onset_bound.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: powered deceleration onset 82 ms after the last valid renewal.")
    check(abs(tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude - 133.6) < 5e-3, "Canon: tau_delay 133.6 ms.")
    check(abs(t_age.to(millisecond).magnitude - 51.6) < 5e-3, "Canon: t_age 51.6 ms.")
    check(abs(eps_sync.to(millisecond).magnitude - 0.2) < 1e-9, "Clock-conversion bound must match the perception contract's 0.2 ms.")
    check(abs(upper_age.magnitude - 51.8) < 5e-3, "Canon (D22): F2 dispatch-age check refuses above a 51.8 ms upper age.")
    check(abs(j_brake.magnitude - 64.0 / 9.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: the jerk bound is the reference polynomial's 7.11 m/s^3 peak.")
    check(abs(budget.magnitude - 968.9925) < 5e-3, "Canon: budget at 1.3 m/s is 968.99 mm.")
    check(abs(spare.magnitude - 131.0075) < 5e-3, "Canon: spare at 1.3 m/s is 131.01 mm.")
    check(abs(c2_distance.magnitude - 605.3125) < 5e-3, "Canon: S-curve stop at 1.3 m/s is 605.31 mm.")
    check(abs(t_spare.magnitude - 100.775) < 5e-3, "Canon: T_latest 100.8 ms.")
    check(abs(ceiling_dry.magnitude - 1.4367) < 5e-5, "Canon: dry-floor ceiling 1.4367 m/s.")
    check(abs(ceiling_insp.magnitude - 1.2309) < 5e-5, "Canon: inspected-floor ceiling 1.2309 m/s.")
    check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Canon: friction needed for a_brake is 0.204.")
    check(abs(bus_min.magnitude - 37.8) < 5e-3, "Canon: the depleted drive bus sags to 37.8 V.")
    check(abs(bus_margin.magnitude - 4.8) < 5e-3, "The sustained screen leaves 4.8 V above the converter lockout.")
    check(abs(i_cross.magnitude - 150.0) < 1e-6, "Reaching the lockout takes a 150 A step.")
    check(bus_min > bus_uvlo, "The load alone cannot cross the lockout, so F4a must inject a supply dip.")
    check(v_aisle < ceiling_dry and ceiling_insp < v_aisle, "Aisle speed sits between the two ceilings.")
    check(budget_insp > d_clear, "At the aisle speed the inspected-floor budget must exceed the clear distance.")
    check(mu_insp < mu_min < mu_dry, "Dry floor supports a_brake; the inspected floor does not.")
    check(t_spare < tau_delay, "A queue shorter than the budgeted pre-brake subtotal exhausts the spare.")
    check(abs(queue_exhaust_ratio - 0.754) < 5e-4, "The exhausting queue is about three-quarters of the pre-brake subtotal.")
    check(abs(overhead.magnitude - 190.0) < 1e-6, "Canon: fixed overhead 190 mm.")
    check(rho_onset.magnitude < 0 and rho_dist.magnitude < 0, "A late onset must drive both F1 margins negative.")
    check(abs(rho_onset_n + 30.0 / 82.0) < 1e-9, "Normalized onset margin is -30/82.")
    check(rho_onset_n < rho_dist_n < 0, "The onset margin dominates the normalized minimum.")
    check(soc_current < 0.05 * i_rail, "The SoC draws a few percent of the rail transient; drive current dominates.")
    check(drive_peak <= i_rail, "Two drive motors at their peak supply most of the transient.")
    check(abs(eps_gap_max - spare.to(meter).magnitude) < 1e-12, "Tolerable discrepancy equals the spare in meters.")
    check(abs(v_takeover.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.8) < 1e-9, "Canon: in-loop takeover speed 0.8 m/s.")
    check(t_spare_takeover >= t_takeover, "At the slowed speed the spare must cover the in-loop takeover.")
    check(t_spare < t_takeover, "At the aisle speed the spare cannot cover the in-loop takeover.")
    check(abs(spare_takeover.magnitude - 530.62) < 5e-2, "Canon: spare at the 0.8 m/s takeover speed is 530.6 mm.")
    check(abs(t_spare_takeover.magnitude - 663.3) < 5e-2, "Canon: T_latest 663.3 ms at 0.8 m/s.")
    check(abs(flag_onset.magnitude - 22.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: stop onset within 22 ms of the flag.")
    check(abs(rail_holdup.to(second).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: permission-rail hold-up 2.0 s.")
    check(abs(flag_to_set.magnitude - 1313.43) < 5e-3, "Canon: flag to brakes set 1313.43 ms.")
    check(abs(holdup_margin.magnitude - 686.57) < 5e-3, "Canon: hold-up margin 686.57 ms.")
    check(v_restricted < ceiling_insp, "The restricted point must sit below the inspected-floor ceiling.")
    check(abs(f1_preonset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-6, "Canon: 82 mm of pre-onset travel at 1.0 m/s.")
    check(abs(f1_c2.magnitude - 507.6) < 5e-2, "Canon: S-curve stop at 1.0 m/s on the inspected floor is 507.6 mm.")
    check(abs(f1_stop_bound.magnitude - 629.6) < 5e-2, "Canon: F1 stop oracle 629.6 mm from the last valid renewal.")
    check(
        abs(f1_aisle_stop_bound.magnitude - 751.9125) < 5e-3 and f1_aisle_stop_bound < budget,
        "F1 stop oracle at 1.3 m/s is 751.91 mm from the last valid renewal.",
    )
    check(
        abs(budget_restricted.magnitude - 831.2) < 5e-2 and budget_restricted < d_clear,
        "Canon: budget at 1.0 m/s on the inspected floor is 831.2 mm.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, precision=1)
    v_drive_str = fmt_velocity(v_drive, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, precision=None)
    a_insp_str = fmt_acceleration(a_insp, precision=2)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    eps_sync_str = fmt_latency(eps_sync, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    upper_age_str = fmt_latency(upper_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=None)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=None)
    t_act_str = fmt_latency(t_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    onset_bound_str = fmt_latency(onset_bound, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    lease_probe_at_str = fmt_latency(lease_probe_at, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    heartbeat_timeout_str = fmt_latency(heartbeat_timeout, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    enforcer_deadline_str = fmt_latency(enforcer_deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_takeover_str = fmt_latency(t_takeover, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_takeover_str = fmt_velocity(v_takeover, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    side_clearance_str = fmt_length(side_clearance, unit=meter, precision=2)
    budget_str = fmt_length(budget, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_spare_str = fmt_latency(t_spare, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    spare_takeover_str = fmt_length(spare_takeover, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_spare_takeover_str = fmt_latency(t_spare_takeover, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    per_ms_str = fmt_length(per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    ceiling_dry_str = fmt_velocity(ceiling_dry, precision=2)
    ceiling_insp_str = fmt_velocity(ceiling_insp, precision=2)
    budget_insp_str = fmt_length(budget_insp, unit=meter, precision=2)
    mu_min_str = fmt(mu_min, precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(mu_dry, precision=2)
    mu_insp_str = fmt(mu_insp, precision=2)
    payload_str = fmt_mass(payload, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    ambient_lo_str = fmt_temperature(ambient_lo, precision=0)
    ambient_hi_str = fmt_temperature(ambient_hi, precision=0)
    bus_nominal_str = fmt_voltage(bus_nominal, precision=1)
    bus_low_str = fmt_voltage(bus_low, precision=0)
    bus_uvlo_str = fmt_voltage(bus_uvlo, precision=0)
    i_rail_str = fmt_current(i_rail, precision=0)
    bus_min_str = fmt_voltage(bus_min, precision=1)
    bus_margin_str = fmt_voltage(bus_margin, precision=1)
    i_cross_str = fmt_current(i_cross, precision=0)
    flag_onset_str = fmt_latency(flag_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    rail_holdup_str = fmt_latency(rail_holdup, unit=second, precision=None)
    flag_to_set_str = fmt_latency(flag_to_set, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    v_restricted_str = fmt_velocity(v_restricted, precision=None)
    f1_stop_bound_str = fmt_length(f1_stop_bound, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    f1_aisle_stop_bound_str = fmt_length(f1_aisle_stop_bound, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    budget_restricted_str = fmt_length(budget_restricted, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    late_onset_str = fmt_latency(late_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    late_extra_str = fmt_length(late_extra, unit=millimeter, precision=None)
    onset_late_str = fmt_latency(onset_late, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    travel_late_str = fmt_length(travel_late, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    rho_onset_str = fmt_time(rho_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0, allow_negative=True)
    rho_dist_str = fmt_length(rho_dist, unit=millimeter, precision=None)
    rho_onset_n_str = fmt(rho_onset_n, precision=3)
    rho_dist_n_str = fmt(rho_dist_n, precision=3)
    soc_power_str = fmt_power(soc_power, unit=ureg.watt, precision=0)
    soc_current_str = fmt_current(soc_current, precision=1)
    drive_peak_str = fmt_current(drive_peak, precision=0)
    soc_share_pct_str = fmt_percent(soc_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    eps_gap_max_str = fmt(eps_gap_max, precision=3)
    queue_exhaust_pct_str = fmt_percent(queue_exhaust_ratio, precision=1, style="prose")
```

The calculations above reproduce the selected partial design budget; they are conditional oracle inputs, not measured timing closure. Its time origin is the exposure midpoint of the qualified observation, whose capture stamp defines the evidence age. The capture-to-admission path still needs a bound for dispatch-to-admission delay. A claim timed from physical target appearance additionally needs the independently witnessed appearance-to-usable-capture interval; that interval is absent from the subtotal. A trial must record successful admission times, continuing evidence age, and physical response onset; the nominal proposal cadence alone does not establish renewal before expiry. The lease begins at successful admission. The renewal campaign must qualify the maximum interval between successful admissions required by @sec-nervous-cadences, including load and rejected proposals, rather than measuring only proposer dispatch. If the missing interval is not covered by a justified allocation, the baseline distance cannot serve as a qualified release bound.

Consider the warehouse mobile manipulator running its aisle at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` (chosen; see the Reader Guide) toward a rack end where a person may step out. The machine's compute stack partitions high-bandwidth neural inference from deterministic safety. An application system-on-chip (SoC) with an embedded accelerator executes the unprivileged vision-language-action chunk policy, while a lockstep safety microcontroller executes the deterministic runtime enforcer. The safety microcontroller commands the base-drive inverters across a hard real-time fieldbus (CAN-FD or EtherCAT), a network whose cyclic frames arrive on a fixed schedule. Both processors draw from the shared `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_nominal_str` drive bus that powers the motors: the application SoC through a converter, and the safety microcontroller through an isolated converter and a held-up permission rail of its own.

Weeks of clean operational runs at that speed say little about four physical hardware and timing faults the design claims to contain:

1. **Proposer Stall (F1):** The neural chunk policy on the application processor renews its capability lease and then suffers a thread deadlock, driver freeze, or thermal throttling stall;
2. **Stale Observation (F2):** A camera frame or depth tensor arrives at the permission path with an aged or corrupted hardware timestamp after buffering in an ISP queue or direct memory access (DMA) ring;
3. **Lost Fieldbus Frames (F3):** Electromagnetic interference (EMI) from inverter switching induces a burst of dropped or corrupted EtherCAT/CAN-FD frames between the safety MCU and drive actuators; and
4. **Drive-Bus Droop & Feed Loss (F4a/F4b):** Motor acceleration current drawn through the pack and harness resistance sags the shared `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_nominal_str` drive bus, or a supply fault interrupts it, and the bus falls below the `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_uvlo_str` lockout of the converter that feeds the application processor.

These failure modes organize the planned physical and authority campaign: physical faults F1–F4 and authority transfer faults A1–A4 (formalized in @tbl-15-fault-classification). Passive logs may contain these faults, but incident-free operation does not establish that the required response was exercised under each one. The lease catches a stall, the evidence-epoch check catches a stale capture time, the drive's fieldbus watchdog catches dropped communication cycles, and the permission path's undervoltage monitor, operating on an electrically isolated, held-up power rail, catches a brownout of the shared drive bus. Each fault is injected at the rack end, alongside the four supervisory authority faults (A1–A4) handed over from @sec-intervention-authority-log, and every stopping trial is scored against formal temporal and distance bounds derived from the machine's physical stopping budget.

An injected fault turns a physical run into a test result that can support an auditable safety case only when the run satisfies the five requirements of the **cyber-physical test contract**:

1. **A bounded claim:** stating the exact invariant the machine must maintain (for the base at the rack end, a stop that ends strictly inside the `{python} RackEndVerification.d_clear_str` clear distance);
2. **Defined test conditions:** specifying the initial speed, payload, floor friction, ambient temperature, bus traffic, and supply-voltage range;
3. **A precommitted oracle\index{Testing!Oracle}:** an automated evaluator that inspects recorded telemetry against the claim without human intervention or post-hoc adjustments;
4. **A stated sampling and injection procedure:** deliberately driving the machine toward its performance limits and injecting physical faults into sensors, buses, power rails, and actuators; and
5. **Provenance\index{Provenance}:** the complete cryptographic metadata record of model weights, calibration tables, sensor serial numbers, oscilloscope traces, and raw bus logs, which permits re-execution under matched declared conditions. Software builds can be reproduced bit for bit; a physical trial can only be repeated under conditions that match within their declared tolerances.

The base's stopping claim and the arm's latch-force claim require separate envelopes, injection points, and pass conditions; this chapter follows the stopping claim. The first decision is where nominal regulation must yield to an independent containment response.

## The Operating Envelope {#sec-verification-operating-envelope}

The **operating envelope**\index{Operating envelope!definition} pairs the target operational design domain (ODD, @sec-evaluation-what-measured) with the machine's internal execution conditions. The same aisle and payload can produce a different response under memory contention, a low supply voltage, or a hot drive. A trial therefore names both the external conditions and the internal load under which its claim must hold.

For the mobile manipulator, the envelope is a set of declared points rather than one nominal condition: the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` aisle speed; payloads of zero and the `{python} RackEndVerification.payload_str` rack capacity; floor friction of at least `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_min_str`, the value the `{python} RackEndVerification.a_brake_str` credible deceleration needs, on dry aisles, and of at least `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str` on floors under the site's inspection regime; and ambient temperatures from `{python} RackEndVerification.ambient_lo_str` to `{python} RackEndVerification.ambient_hi_str`. For inspected floors the envelope declares a restricted point at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_restricted_str`, the candidate restricted configuration whose friction premise the enforcement record states (@sec-enforcement-telemetry), and trials there use a test floor whose measured friction sits at the `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str` qualification value, so that the stop they exercise is the one friction bounds.

Each point is paired with the machine's internal execution state: application-processor load up to its peak neural inference burst, the drive bus anywhere from its `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_low_str` depleted point to its `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_nominal_str` nominal, EtherCAT/CAN-FD transmission jitter, memory crossbar contention, and the safety microcontroller's thermal state. The campaign also challenges the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_takeover_str` moving-takeover candidate with its `{python} RackEndVerification.t_takeover_str` takeover interval. This is a rejected rack-end candidate, not an admitted operating mode: @sec-intervention-authority-transitions requires the local stop first when that transition cannot preserve the stopping envelope.

An operating envelope is distinct from the larger **survival envelope**\index{Survival envelope!definition} that encloses it. Inside the operating envelope the learned policy and the tracking controllers regulate the process. When a disturbance, a sensor failure, or a compute stall pushes the machine across that boundary, nominal regulation is conceded, and the objective becomes bringing the body to a bounded, safe state before structural limits are breached. For the mobile manipulator, the survival envelope must be established for each selected response and machine state (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder). The normal resident stop uses powered deceleration and applies holding brakes at standstill. Torque inhibit is a different response and does not inherit that stopping-distance budget. Beyond it lies structural failure, where stored kinetic energy ($E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$) exceeds what the hardware can dissipate before physical impact.

Defining the boundary of the operating envelope requires deriving limits from first principles rather than asserting convenient software timeouts. At the rack end the limit is the stopping budget. Stopping distance grows linearly with the pre-brake delay and quadratically with speed (@eq-body-stopping-distance), and the conditional design budget of @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes (@tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget), with its `{python} RackEndVerification.tau_delay_str` capture-referenced pre-brake subtotal, the smooth resident stop that @sec-planning-behavior-seam commits to, and the tracking inset, gives a partial-budget ceiling of `{python} RackEndVerification.ceiling_dry_str` on a dry floor before the unresolved dispatch-to-admission interval is charged. At the candidate `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` this subtotal needs `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_str` of the `{python} RackEndVerification.d_clear_str` clear distance and leaves `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str` before that missing interval and the required positive release reserve are allocated, a distance it covers in `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str`.

Two conditional oracle bounds follow. Before a trial, its record must establish that the intervals in the bound cover the tested path; any unresolved allocation remains a qualification gap:

1. **Powered Deceleration Onset Deadline:** Powered deceleration onset must come no later than `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` after the last valid renewal, traversing the lease path of @sec-nervous-cadences: the `{python} RackEndVerification.t_lease_str` lease, one `{python} RackEndVerification.t_tick_str` tick of the permission loop, one `{python} RackEndVerification.t_bus_str` bus cycle, and `{python} RackEndVerification.t_act_str` from delivered stop command to powered deceleration onset. (The power-rail faults of F4 take their onset from the undervoltage flag instead).
2. **Stopping Distance Bound:** The physical stop, measured by external optical ground-truth instruments independent of the machine, must end within the distance allowed from the same event the fault is referenced to. The `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_str` subtotal starts at the qualified observation's exposure midpoint and omits dispatch-to-admission delay. It is not a bound from an arbitrary target appearance. An appearance-referenced trial must independently timestamp the physical appearance and the first usable capture, charge the intervening travel together with dispatch-to-admission travel, and precommit a full bound against the clearance measured at appearance. A capture-referenced trial instead uses clearance and external position at capture; neither trial may score a physical pass from the incomplete subtotal. A stalled proposer offers no target appearance, so its stop, like its onset, is measured from the last valid renewal: the travel during the `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` before powered deceleration onset, the resident stop, and the tracking inset give `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_aisle_stop_bound_str` at the aisle speed.

Both bounds presume that the permission path, required sensing, and powered drive survive the injected fault. Logic and brake-coil hold-up do not supply drive energy; F4b must retain and measure a separately justified drive supply and energy-absorption path throughout deceleration. If the fault removes those resources, the trial challenges a different fallback whose stopping envelope must be established separately. Neither bound depends on a further proposer response. A chunk policy that stalls cannot delay powered deceleration onset, because the stop begins when the lease expires rather than when the proposer notices, so a test of F1 measures the permission path and not the policy. The budget protects a static obstacle at the clear distance, and a trial against a static target says nothing about a person still walking toward the machine, a premise the site's crossing rule carries (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion).

## One F1 Trial from Injection to Record {#sec-verification-f1-trial}

For F1 we choose the restricted envelope point at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_restricted_str` with the declared payload and inspected-floor friction. The claim is conditional: the permission path and drive remain able to execute the resident powered stop after proposal renewal ceases. The test kills or freezes the proposer just after its last valid renewal while leaving its timer heartbeat alive. That separates progress of the proposer from liveness of an unrelated interrupt.

A physical rig containing the production base, drive, loaded body, and qualified test floor can exercise the complete stopping claim. A processor bench can challenge lease expiry but substitutes the plant; a simulation substitutes both target timing and mechanics. Neither alone supplies the required physical distance witness. The containment fixture must protect the test area independently of the response under test.

The F1 reference event is the last successful admission that renewed the lease, not proposer dispatch or the later injection trigger. The trace must retain the admission and injection events. Independent channels record lease expiry, the permission-path stop command, powered deceleration onset, and external position through standstill. Drive current or torque together with wheel motion witnesses powered onset; a brake contact switch witnesses the subsequent holding-brake application. A contact switch alone cannot timestamp the beginning of powered braking.

Recording the state trajectory, the detector identity, the refusal timestamp, and the time to restore the bounded state requires instrumentation electrically and logically independent of the machine, such as optical shaft encoders and high-speed cameras on isolated digitizers. An onboard logging daemon is corrupted by the very failure it tries to capture, because a faulted processor or a saturated bus delays log serialization.[^fn-hw-trace-instrumentation] Independent measurement also rejects false passes, in which the machine survived for reasons absent from the safety claim. An injected lost-frame fault can trip an unmonitored thermal breaker or an auxiliary ground loop that drops power to the drives, so that the spring-applied brake stops the base inside the budget while the software enforcer has deadlocked in a priority inversion. An oracle that inspects only stopping distance scores that trial a pass. The test framework must verify that the enforcer path named in the safety claim executed the corrective action.

[^fn-hw-trace-instrumentation]: **Non-Intrusive Hardware Tracing**\index{Hardware tracing!CoreSight ETM}: Non-intrusive tracing utilizes dedicated silicon hardware debug blocks (such as ARM CoreSight Embedded Trace Macrocell) and external field-programmable gate array (FPGA) bus sniffers that snoop internal bus transactions without stealing CPU execution cycles. By buffering execution traces in dedicated high-speed SRAM decoupled from the system memory bus, hardware analyzers capture cycle-accurate fault-reaction timestamps without perturbing real-time thread schedules. Relying on software logging daemons introduces the **probe effect**\index{Probe effect} [@gait1986probe]: the instrumentation changes the timing it observes, so logging overhead can mask or create the race conditions under test.

A liveness signal is another source of false passes, so the test must target what it can miss. @Sec-nervous-hardware-isolation recounts the mechanism a plaintiff expert argued in the Toyota unintended-acceleration litigation [@barr2013toyota], a timer interrupt that kept servicing the watchdog while control tasks could die, and draws the rule that a timer feed proves only that the feed path ran (\ref{psp-verification-watchdog-liveness}, \ref{ws-verification-toyota-unintended-acceleration-limits-task-blind}). The test vector for that rule kills the control task, or freezes its output, while the timer interrupt stays alive, and measures the actuator command and the watchdog output on instruments independent of the controller. On the mobile manipulator, F1 is this vector applied to the proposer. The host heartbeat can keep reporting a live process after the chunk-policy task has died, so F1 passes on powered deceleration onset measured at the drive, never on a heartbeat in a log. Because the historical mechanism is attributed rather than established, a bench result speaks for the design under test, not for any vehicle.

::: {#psp-verification-watchdog-liveness .callout-perspective title="The watchdog liveness invariant"}
A watchdog fed by a periodic timer interrupt shows only that the interrupt handler executed, not that safety-critical application tasks met their deadlines or executed without corruption. A qualified fault injection campaign explicitly isolates task progress from timer liveness, testing physical shutdown under task death, thread starvation, and frozen control registers.
:::

::: {#ws-verification-toyota-unintended-acceleration-limits-task-blind .callout-war-story title="Testing a task-blind watchdog hypothesis"}
**Context**: In *Bookout v. Toyota* (Oklahoma County, 2013), a jury heard expert testimony on the electronic throttle control system (ETCS-i) of a 2005 Camry. The plaintiffs' software expert argued that safety-critical control tasks could fail silently while the supervision meant to catch them stayed alive [@barr2013toyota].

**Mechanism**: The engine controller serviced its hardware watchdog from a recurring timer-tick interrupt rather than from evidence that the control tasks had run. The expert testified that if one task that handled throttle control and several failsafes died, through memory corruption or a stack overflow, the throttle could stick at its last computed command while the timer interrupt kept feeding the watchdog [@barr2013toyota]. The design also carried a second, monitor CPU, but he argued that it could not see which tasks were running, that it detected this task's death only indirectly, when the driver changed the brake pedal's state, and that a single analog-to-digital converter digitized the accelerator-pedal position for both processors, a common cause that a fault on the main processor could share [@dunn2013toyota]. Recovery could therefore require the counterintuitive act of lifting a foot off the brake during the event.

**Impact**: On October 24, 2013, the jury awarded \$3 million in compensatory damages and found that Toyota had acted with reckless disregard; the parties settled before the jury could consider punitive damages [@srs2013toyota]. The verdict did not establish a technical cause. The NASA engineering review for the federal investigation found no evidence that an electronic malfunction caused large unintended accelerations [@nasa2011toyota]. It did document electronic faults, among them a tin whisker that formed a 248 Ω short in an accelerator-pedal position sensor from a 2003 Camry, a fault that, in vehicle tests, changed how the throttle followed the pedal but still let it close whenever the pedal was released [@leidecker2011tinwhisker]. The investigation attributed the incidents it could explain to floor-mat entrapment, sticking pedals, and pedal misapplication.

**Response**: For the design under test, fault injection must establish which application progress checks reach the watchdog, whether the independent monitor shares any input path with the processor it supervises (@sec-verification-forward-analysis), and which protective input can still command a physically suitable response. The historical case does not establish those properties for the warehouse machine.

**Systems lesson**: A periodic liveness feed proves only that the timer loop ran, not that control tasks executed correctly. Engineers must verify fault detection using end-to-end hardware injection that kills application tasks while measuring physical actuator arrest on independent instrumentation.
:::

The intervention mechanism must be tested under the conditions that make intervention necessary. An enforcer that takes over cleanly on an idle bench provides no evidence for production, where in a crisis the policy runs at peak throughput, memory buses carry high-resolution sensor streams, DMA channels move frame buffers, and the base carries its loaded rack at the aisle speed. The framework injects faults under the declared thermal and electrical load and measures both lease-expiry revocation and, separately, the time from a diagnostic flag to powered deceleration onset at the drive. If the intervention path shares a bus arbiter with the neural accelerator, the takeover can stall behind a burst transfer that cannot be preempted, and a safety case that assumed instantaneous takeover fails in the field if the takeover was verified only on a quiet bus.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Microarchitectural stress patterns build directly on the memory contention benchmarks from @sec-placement-resource-contention.
:::

A campaign runs every injection under one fixed protocol, so that a verdict follows from the procedure rather than from whoever reads the trace. The test orchestrator first checks every precondition, such as temperature, rail voltage, and wheel speed, against its declared tolerance, in that quantity's unit, and a trial that starts outside tolerance ends as `INVALID` before any fault is injected. It then brings the logic analyzer, the plant, and the truth digitizers onto one reference clock, lets the base settle at its envelope point, and fires the injection on a trigger line that stamps the fault's start on that clock. The isolated analyzer retains that stamp and the claim's reference event, such as F1's last valid renewal, so detector, drive takeover, and standstill intervals can be scored from the correct origin, while truth sensors wired to a crowbar relay can cut actuator power if the base leaves the survival envelope. The precommitted oracle scores the trace from the independent truth instruments under the verdicts and pass rule of @sec-verification-oracles-acceptance, and incomplete truth frames surface only at this stage, after the injection has run, as `UNOBSERVABLE`. The orchestrator signs the record's header and binds it to the evidence bundle by digest.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Protocol:** @Sec-appendix-systems-fault-protocol gives the protocol stage by stage, with its error codes, for a reader building the test orchestrator.
:::

## Fault Oracles and Acceptance {#sec-verification-oracles-acceptance}

The F1 trace must establish both timely onset and bounded travel; a stopped base alone establishes neither. Without an oracle fixed in advance, engineers judge time-series plots after the run from gross symptoms, such as whether Joule heating\index{Joule heating!component failure} melted a phase wire or a controller threw an unhandled exception, and the test becomes an anecdote. An **oracle**\index{Oracle!definition} is the predicate, defined in full before the run, that scores a trial against its claim.

### Four-verdict test oracles and forensic integrity {#sec-verification-four-verdicts}

Scoring also needs an **invalid-test rule**\index{Invalid-test rule!definition} for a run the environment failed to deliver. If a traction-control derate on a floor joint slows the base before the injection, so that it meets the fault below its declared test speed, the trial did not test the envelope point it claims. If the frame injector overflows its own queue and drops the fault packet before it reaches the transceiver, the machine never met the disturbance. Scoring such a run as a pass manufactures confidence, and scoring it as a failure blames the machine for the fixture. The oracle therefore returns one of four verdicts. `PASS` means every precommitted predicate held; `FAIL` means a measured predicate was violated; `INVALID` means the injection or a precondition failed; and `UNOBSERVABLE` means the truth data needed to score the trial were lost, with the partial trace retained. Under either of these last two verdicts a field the trial did not measure is marked unavailable, never zero. Neither verdict ever counts as `PASS`, and neither is dropped from the coverage report. An `UNOBSERVABLE` trial is therefore a defect of the test harness, not an ambiguous pass. Treating an unobservable run as a success, or silently discarding runs with dropped telemetry from test reports, introduces survivorship bias: if an electrical transient causes an EMI burst that crashes the logging DAQ, discarding that trial conceals the exact vulnerability under test. Forensic integrity requires reporting all four verdicts explicitly.

Precommitment separates evidence from post-hoc storytelling. Fault-injection behavior is noisy and surprising, and criteria negotiated after the trace is seen drift to fit it. An overrun is explained away as floor variation, or an onset later than the `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` bound is excused because the base still stopped short of the rack end.

The precommitted record fixes the physical predicates, physical units and any normalization scales, response-time bounds, and invalidation triggers before the first injection. The evaluator retains a signed margin for each predicate and returns `PASS` only if every required margin and timing bound passes. If the stop exceeds its bound by a few millimeters or powered deceleration onset misses its deadline by $2\text{ ms}$, the record states which measured predicate failed; the trace and follow-up analysis determine whether floor friction, brake lag, derating, or a diagnostic delay caused it. Precommitment is where principle \ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority} first binds a test. Release will grant authority on these records, so a verdict scored by a rule revised after the trace was seen would grant authority on the strength of an outcome rather than a test.

### The F1 record and its missing coverage {#sec-verification-manifest-coverage}

A **fault record**\index{Fault record!definition} binds a fixed header to the independently retained trace. The header holds the fields every trial shares. Its identity fields name the trial and its claim, the envelope point, the injected fault by mode, magnitude, and target, and a digest of the precommitted oracle. Its outcome fields carry the measured detection and takeover times, the signed margin for the claim, the verdict status, the digest of the evidence bundle, and a signature over the header. The variable trace stays in the bundle.

The planned F1 record at the envelope's restricted point, `{python} RackEndVerification.v_restricted_str` on an inspected floor, with the rack loaded to `{python} RackEndVerification.payload_str`, specifies those fields (@tbl-15-f1-record). As for every stall, the distance oracle is referenced to the last valid renewal. The travel during the `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` before powered deceleration onset, the resident stop on a floor of friction `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str`, and the tracking inset together give `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_stop_bound_str`, shorter than the `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_restricted_str` capture-referenced subtotal at that speed. The latter includes earlier evidence age and fixed geometric allowances, omits dispatch-to-admission travel, and cannot be substituted for F1's renewal-referenced oracle or for an appearance-referenced bound. The outcome field holds no value and is marked unavailable. No trial in this book has been run, so the field names the measurement that will fill it, and until that measurement exists the record carries no verdict.

| Trial and claim                                                                                | Envelope point                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | Oracle, predeclared from the last valid renewal                                                                                                        | Detector and witness                                                                             | Outcome to be measured                                                                                                 | Verdict                                                        |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|
| F1, proposer stall: chunk-policy task killed one tick after a renewal; rack-end stopping claim | `{python} RackEndVerification.v_restricted_str`; `{python} RackEndVerification.payload_str` payload; test floor measured at $\mu =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str`; drive bus at `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_nominal_str` nominal | Powered deceleration onset $\le$ `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str`; travel to rest $\le$ `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_stop_bound_str` | Lease timer on the permission path; expiry, revocation, and onset each on its own wire and clock | Trial count; maximum onset and maximum travel over the trials, each with its signed margin; unavailable until measured | None until scored; `PASS` only if both margins are nonnegative |

: **One F1 fault record at the restricted envelope point**: The header fields of a proposer-stall trial on the warehouse mobile manipulator, with the oracle fixed before the run and the outcome left as the measurement that must fill it. {#tbl-15-f1-record tbl-colwidths="[18,22,18,14,16,12]"}

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Byte layout:** @Sec-appendix-systems-wire-fault lays out the header field by field, including how an unavailable value is encoded, for a reader building the ledger.
:::

The record keeps the four verdicts distinct field by field. A breaker that prevents the requested injection makes the trial `INVALID`, and for a trial aborted before injection the detection time, takeover time, and margin are unavailable rather than zero; the bundle records a validity flag for each measured field and why it is absent, and the oracle checks those flags and the verdict before doing any arithmetic, so an unavailable field never enters a pass count or a latency or margin statistic.

A single aggregate percentage hides where the campaign never went. A machine that survived 98 percent of five thousand fault trials has shown little if all five thousand ran at room temperature on a quiet memory bus. Coverage is therefore reported along separate dimensions: functional safety requirements, physical envelope boundaries, physical and logical injection sites, timing tails, hardware build revisions, and multi-fault combinations. For the mobile manipulator, boundary coverage tracks whether faults were injected with the rack empty and full, at the aisle speed on dry floors and at the restricted speed on inspected ones, and with the drive bus at its depleted point. Timing tail coverage isolates injections targeting the $P_{99}$ scheduling latency of the permission loop and peak direct memory access utilization. A machine achieves acceptable verification not when an average coverage index exceeds an arbitrary threshold, but when the minimum coverage across every individual dimension satisfies the requirements of the safety case.[^fn-std-iso-injection]

[^fn-std-iso-injection]: **Scope of assurance standards**\index{ISO 26262!Hardware Fault Injection}: ISO 26262-5 addresses road-vehicle electrical and electronic hardware. Its single-point and latent fault metrics concern the architecture and its allocated safety goals; they are not the aggregate $C_{\text{diag}}$ of \ref{nbk-verification-hardware-fault-injection-coverage-mean-time}. Fault injection is one way to test diagnostic assumptions, alongside analysis and other evidence. ANSI/UL 4600 frames an autonomous-vehicle safety case from multiple kinds of evidence. Neither standard makes a fixed number of HIL trials sufficient for release.

Repeated trials count only where something varies. A deterministic fault script run five hundred times on a digital bench, with fixed initial conditions, register states, clock dividers, and inputs, executes the same branch sequence every time and says no more than one run. On the test aisle, repetition samples floor friction, asynchronous interrupt arrivals, bus arbitration, and the phase between the sensor clock and the inference cycle, so it measures the spread and tail of the response-time distribution.

## Extending the Trial to the Envelope {#sec-verification-extending-trial}

The F1 record specifies one experiment and honestly leaves its outcome empty. A campaign must extend that experiment across the coupled conditions in the operating envelope and derive different injections for the other claims.

### Multi-dimensional boundary coupling versus scalar sweeps {#sec-verification-boundary-coupling}

On the mobile manipulator, separate minimum and maximum values for individual variables miss the true operating boundary, because physical, computational, and electrical conditions are coupled. Sweeping one variable at a time with the others held at nominal values leaves the coupled corners untested:

- The `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` aisle speed and an inspected floor with friction `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str` each lie inside their declared individual ranges, yet together they fall outside the envelope. On that floor friction, not the brake, sets the credible deceleration, which drops to `{python} RackEndVerification.a_insp_str`. The resident stop lengthens, and the budget at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` grows to `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_insp_str`, past the `{python} RackEndVerification.d_clear_str` clear distance; the speed boundary on that floor is `{python} RackEndVerification.ceiling_insp_str`, which is why the envelope's restricted point sits below it.
- Contact non-linearities exacerbate this coupling. On real warehouse surfaces, friction is not an idealized constant scalar $\mu$; it is a non-linear, dynamic contact state governed by surface contamination (concrete dust, moisture, or oil sheens), wheel tread temperature, and dynamic load transfer. Under rapid braking, longitudinal load transfer shifts normal force from the rear to the front axle ($F_{z, \text{front}} = m g \frac{l_r}{L} + m a \frac{h}{L}$), where $l_r$ is the center-of-mass distance from the rear axle, $L$ is the wheelbase, $h$ is the center-of-mass height, and $a$ is the positive deceleration magnitude. The rear wheels lose normal load and can reach the tire's traction limit. If the policy commands deceleration assuming peak dry friction, the unweighted wheels can slip, reducing effective braking traction. In the constant-friction approximation, stopping distance grows inversely with available friction and quadratically with speed ($d_{\text{stop}} \sim v^2 / 2\mu g$).
- Computational and electrical conditions couple the same way. A heavy vision-language-action forward pass on the application SoC saturates its shared memory, delaying camera-buffer processing and the compact evidence handoff to the safety microcontroller, which lengthens the perceptual lag $\tau_{\text{delay}}$. Because stopping distance grows linearly with that lag (@eq-body-stopping-distance), a `{python} RackEndVerification.late_onset_str` memory stall consumes `{python} RackEndVerification.late_extra_str` of clearance at the aisle speed. The electrical coupling runs through the drive, not the accelerator. At its `{python} RackEndVerification.soc_power_str` maximum the SoC draws about `{python} RackEndVerification.soc_current_str` from the depleted bus, `{python} RackEndVerification.soc_share_pct_str` of the `{python} RackEndVerification.i_rail_str` transient; the two drive motors at their peak supply up to `{python} RackEndVerification.drive_peak_str` of it. Hard acceleration therefore sags the shared bus through the pack and harness resistance, and an inference burst matters instead on the SoC's own point-of-load regulator, a separate transient that the F4 campaign must measure separately.
- Payload and posture couple to the stopping limit through stability as well as friction. With the arm raised over a loaded rack the center of mass rises, and a quasi-static base tips forward once its deceleration exceeds $g\,b/h$, where $b$ is the horizontal distance from the center of mass to the front support line and $h$ its height. That limit can bind before friction does, and ISO 3691-4 requires stability to be verified for driverless industrial trucks [@iso3691part4]. The machine's record does not yet carry a measured center-of-mass height, so the envelope cannot yet state whether the credible deceleration clears this limit; a tilt-table or corner-scale measurement of the loaded machine would supply it.
- Thermal throttling can delay proposal generation and reduce useful service. With an independent, valid resident stop, a missed renewal invokes the bounded fallback rather than indefinitely extending the stopping delay. The compound test must determine whether shared power, sensing, or bus interference also compromises that fallback. Payload matters because the credible deceleration is declared for the loaded machine; unloaded trials cannot establish it.

### Physical perturbations versus digital adversarial noise {#sec-verification-physical-perturbations}

A pixel perturbation and a physical disturbance exercise different interfaces. A tensor-level test can isolate model sensitivity, while an optical test also exercises the lens, exposure control, sensor, and timestamp path. Neither substitutes for the other, and the threat model must state whether the attacker can change digital packets, the physical scene, or both.

For the rack-end claim, useful physical disturbances include glare that obscures the obstacle, vibration that corrupts motion sensing, and a floor transition that reduces available traction. Each needs a realizable injection and an independent witness: illumination measured at the sensor, reference motion independent of onboard odometry, or a qualified friction measurement. A well-formed sensor packet does not establish that its physical interpretation is correct.

### What the envelope claim leaves open {#sec-verification-falsification-formulation}

Boundary testing searches for counterexamples to a declared claim. For F1, the first useful experiment needs no optimizer: stop renewal while the base moves, then independently measure when deceleration starts and where the base comes to rest. Later searches vary the initial state and injection phase to challenge smaller margins (@sec-verification-falsification-trajectory-formulation). Formal analysis, simulation, and physical testing contribute different evidence; none repairs an omitted premise by itself.

A boundary stays honest only if every parameter carries its unit, its provenance, its calibrated uncertainty, and an engineer accountable for it. A credible deceleration of `{python} RackEndVerification.a_brake_str` is incomplete until the record says whether it came from stopping trials at the loaded mass, a drive datasheet, or a friction model, and with what resolution the external distance reference measured each stop. A new wheel tread compound or new EtherCAT slave firmware obliges that owner to re-evaluate whether the boundary has moved.

Testing the envelope means attacking its boundary surface. Interior points, where the base crawls unloaded across a dry floor on fresh camera frames, show only that the machine works under ideal conditions. The test framework places points on, just inside, and just outside each consequential boundary. Points just inside check that the policy keeps closed-loop stability\index{Closed-loop stability} under the largest permitted stress; points on the boundary check that margins survive nominal sensor noise; points just outside check that the enforcer takes authority from the policy predictably and halts the base within the survival envelope before the clear distance is gone.

A hardware malfunction and a functional insufficiency require different challenges. A sensor can deliver intact packets while glare defeats its obstacle estimate. The campaign must therefore test both failure of the execution mechanism and failure of the information on which that mechanism depends. Naming an enforcer does not establish that it can detect a physically unobservable condition; the claim may require a narrower operating envelope.

::: {#psp-verification-hardware-falsification .callout-perspective title="The hardware falsification principle"}
A hardware-dependent safety claim needs an observable challenge to its physical premises\index{Fault injection!hardware}. If the campaign cannot inject the relevant disturbance or retain the required witness, the record must preserve that verification gap.
:::

Once every constraint, latency budget, and environmental limit is stated as a number, the design claims of the preceding chapters become targets for fault injection\index{Fault injection}, each with a threshold that must trigger protective intervention\index{Protective intervention}.

## Deriving the Fault List {#sec-verification-deriving-fault-list}

F1 came from negating one claim: proposal renewal continues within its lease. The rest of the fault list has two sources. Inverting design records tests the assumptions the architecture names; working forward from mechanics, power distribution, and human interaction finds hazards the records may have omitted.

### Inverting design records and the five-element chain {#sec-verification-inverting-records}

The first source of faults is the design records, inverted. @Sec-data through @sec-evaluation state the learned policy's properties: its training distribution, its state-action assumptions, and its inference latency ceilings. @Sec-perception through @sec-placement state interface and execution properties such as bus allocations, observation freshness, and estimation bounds, and @sec-intervention states how quickly authority can leave a failing policy and who holds the override. If the machine's records state that the chunk policy renews its proposal every `{python} RackEndVerification.chunk_period_str` at every speed up to the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_drive_str` drive limit, the verification suite inverts that claim by injecting stalled renewals, delayed observations, and out-of-range encoder readings to test whether the permission path detects the violation within its budget.

For a single fault, the bounded claim and the injection procedure of that list become a **five-element chain**:

1. **The negated condition:** the exact architectural or timing invariant violated (e.g., proposal renewal halted after lease issue);
2. **The physical injection point:** the exact hardware or bus interface where the disturbance enters (e.g., inline FPGA serializer, CAN-FD disturbance node, or programmable DC load);
3. **The expected detector:** the deterministic monitoring primitive tasked with catching the violation (e.g., lease countdown timer or evidence-epoch comparator);
4. **The bounded response:** the deterministic transition executed by the enforcer (e.g., revoking proposal authority and commanding the resident stop suffix); and
5. **The observable pass condition:** the quantitative, independently witnessed metric that scores the trial (for F1 at aisle speed, onset $\le$ `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` and travel from renewal $\le$ `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_aisle_stop_bound_str`).

A recorded design property becomes a testable fault only when all five elements are defined and observable. When any element of this chain cannot be defined or measured, the architecture contains a **verification gap**\index{Verification gap!definition}. A verification gap indicates that the claim cannot be falsified by test. Such gaps cannot be ignored; they require dedicated hardware instrumentation (such as external optical trackers or non-intrusive trace macros), a narrower operational claim, or a redesign of the execution path.

Inversion also reaches the learned proposer's assumptions, because distribution shift can create a functional insufficiency even when every frame arrives intact. A chunk policy trained in simulation on dry concrete with friction `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_dry_str` proposes decelerations that a floor at `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str` turns into wheel slip. Inverting that evaluation claim means injecting the unmodeled traction. Sensor bias and data perturbations are injected for the same reason, because a policy with a high nominal reward can still command jittering actuators once its inputs are perturbed. A permissive execution path can then fail on valid, uncorrupted commands, because software and mechanics stay coupled across the causal boundary (@sec-boundary-causal-boundary).

At each inter-module contract, the fault list negates the property at its physical point of handoff: observation freshness, state validity, intent lifetime, planning deadlines, enforcement independence, and resource allocation. For the `{python} RackEndVerification.t_lease_str` chunk lease of @sec-nervous-cadences, the test environment replays the expired admitted record `{python} RackEndVerification.lease_probe_at_str` after its last renewal and confirms that the permission path refuses to extend authority from that record. A new proposal at the same time is a separate admission attempt: it must pass the current evidence, state, mode, and stopping-reserve checks before it can receive a new lease. For the enforcer's claimed independence from the policy computer, the test saturates the shared memory bus with DMA traffic and confirms that the enforcer still meets its `{python} RackEndVerification.enforcer_deadline_str` deadline inside each `{python} RackEndVerification.t_tick_str` tick. The discipline cuts both ways. Bus starvation, clock skew, and supply fluctuation are injected where the design claims tolerance, because a fault drawn from a generic menu invents a requirement the machine was never specified to meet.

Inversion has a structural limit. It produces only the faults the design team already modeled, so the list is only as complete as the design claims. If no record says how the base's spring-applied brake behaves when its lining glazes after repeated stops, there is nothing to invert, and the failure never reaches the suite.

### Forward physical analysis and common-cause modes {#sec-verification-forward-analysis}

A second, independent source works forward from the physical machine, enumerating what the body, the power network, the floor, and the environment can do regardless of what the software believes. Wheels skid when a commanded deceleration exceeds what the floor can transmit; brake linings glaze under repeated stops; tires wear and change the rolling radius that odometry assumes; drive vibration loosens a camera mount until its calibration drifts. These hazards originate in mechanics and tribology, outside every abstraction the software reasons over. Leveson's **Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP)**\index{Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes!definition} framework[^fn-std-stpa-leveson] [@leveson2011engineering] brings them into hazard analysis.

For example, start with a drive that continues producing torque after a stop command. A stuck enable or failed power stage may defeat the normal powered suffix. The test must independently observe delivered torque, motion, and the secondary isolation path. Safe torque off can remove drive torque, but it does not establish the normal stopping distance or hold a gravity-loaded joint. The record must name a separately justified containment response and its physical oracle; if none exists, the fault exposes an architectural gap rather than inheriting the normal stop budget.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_fault_injection_coverage_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Vertical ladder showing fault injection climbing from SRAM bit-flips up to physical dyno shaft jamming."}

*Fault injection climbs from software bit-flips to physical dyno shaft jamming.*
:::

[^fn-std-stpa-leveson]: **STAMP/STPA Hazard Analysis**\index{Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis!emergent hazards}: Developed at MIT by Nancy Leveson, STAMP treats safety as a control problem rather than a component-reliability problem, so hazards appear as unsafe control actions at interfaces, such as a seam where bus latency or filter lag erodes a stability margin. STPA is the hazard-analysis method built on it.

Working forward exposes fault classes that no software record implies: clock loss, brownouts that leave logic levels between valid thresholds, drive-switching interference coupling into encoder lines, corrupted configuration memory, and reset lines that bridge domains meant to be independent. If the safety microcontroller and the application processor shared one power-management IC, an undervoltage transient during a drive-current surge could reset both processors at the moment the proposer loses control. No software record contains that failure, because each module assumes its supply is ideal. An enforcer cannot arrest a failing policy if it shares the supply that browns out with it; the safety runtime must outlive the faulted workload it supervises, powered from an isolated, held-up auxiliary supply.

Forward analysis also tests the common-cause independence claims of @sec-nervous and @sec-placement. Two paths isolated on a diagram often share one physical vulnerability, as when the lidar and a redundant bumper switch are routed through one cable carrier, share an analog reference inside one converter, or are built on timer silicon with the same errata. A transient that latches up both channels at once defeats any argument that treats their failures as independent. **Common-cause analysis**\index{Common-cause analysis!definition} traces routing, power paths, and clock trees so that no single physical event can disable both the policy and the intervention mechanism.

The physical source extends to operator error and foreseeable misuse (@sec-intervention). Floor staff jumper a rack-end presence sensor during maintenance, park a pallet jack across a marked crossing, or unplug a warning beacon to silence it, while remote assistants request speeds the aisle does not allow. When a remote assistant commands the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_drive_str` drive limit in the aisle, the verification framework must verify that the command is denied by capability, or limited under an active `manual_drive` entry to the admitted manual mode's speed, and that the permission check runs on it like any other proposal.

Working forward from the physical machine adds one representative mechanical class, the actuator jam, to the record-derived list in @tbl-15-fault-classification. Completeness still requires a separate hazard-analysis argument for the specified plant and operating envelope.

### Transduction-layer cyber-physical attacks {#sec-verification-transduction-attacks}

The optical, acoustic, and contact disturbances introduced with the operating envelope also become **transduction-layer cyber-physical attacks**\index{Cyber-physical security!transduction attacks}\index{Sensor spoofing!physical injection}\index{Cybersecurity engineering!ISO/SAE 21434} when an adversary induces them. Their verification consequence is the same: a sensor can deliver a well-formed packet whose physical claim is false. Packet integrity therefore cannot serve as the oracle for perception validity.

For an optical disturbance, the test must specify the illumination and approach conditions that challenge the obstacle claim, the cross-sensor plausibility check expected to detect the discrepancy, and the fallback response. An independent tracker measures the obstacle clearance and the base's motion while the camera remains disturbed. The fault record must distinguish a detected anomaly followed by a bounded stop from a missed obstacle that happened not to cause contact. If the detector cannot distinguish the disturbed signal from valid evidence, that operating condition remains a verification gap; naming a protective monitor does not establish that it will fire.

### Choosing the injection phase {#sec-verification-fault-optimization}

A stall just after renewal exercises almost the full remaining lease; a stall near expiry exercises the transition between proposal and fallback. The campaign records the injection phase rather than treating repeated injections as equivalent. Automated search can later vary phase, duration, and intensity using the oracle's measured margin (@sec-verification-falsification-trajectory-formulation).

Besides inverted claims and forward hazards, the fault list must test the authority cases A1–A4 of @sec-intervention-authority-log, each a row of @tbl-15-fault-classification, tested with the machine in the state that makes intervention urgent, the loaded base approaching the rack end. The campaign tests requests at the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_takeover_str` moving-takeover candidate and at the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` aisle speed. Their partial-budget waiting allowances are `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_takeover_str` and `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str`, respectively, before the missing timing interval and transition costs are charged. These values do not admit either moving handover. For the rack-end case, @sec-intervention-authority-transitions requires rejecting the infeasible transition and dispatching the local stop before its deadline; manual operation can begin only after a separately checked handover in its admitted mode. A trial conducted only with the base parked cannot establish that rejection and stopping occurred soon enough during approach.
