### Compound faults and coupled disturbances {#sec-verification-compound-faults}

Each row of @tbl-15-fault-classification injects one disturbance, yet a machine in operation rarely meets one at a time. Combining rows at random would multiply the list without finding the combinations that matter, so coupled disturbances are enumerated from shared causes instead. The test ledger of the placement record (@sec-placement-hardware-allocation) names every resource that the permission path shares with the learned workloads, and each shared rail, clock, or bus becomes one compound fault, injected at the cause rather than at its symptoms.

For the running machine, the declared transient at the depleted point leaves the illustrative bus at `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_min_str`, `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_margin_str` above the converter lockout; only a `{python} RackEndVerification.i_cross_str` step or a supply fault reaches the lockout, so F4a injects the dip rather than the load alone. A compound trial must measure the delivered waveform and the effects on the proposer, sensors, drive logic, and independent witnesses. It cannot infer simultaneous resets or frozen frames from the commanded load alone.

A droop on a shared rail can slow the enforcer, freeze a sensor at a plausible value, and reset the logger in the same interval. A burst on a shared bus ages observations while it delays the permission path's own reads and the heartbeat that would reveal the delay. A fault in a shared clock skews the timestamps of every record that crosses the proposal boundary at once, so freshness checks pass on data that is already old. The oracle for a compound fault therefore checks the protective response against its deadline and also checks that the evidence needed to judge that response survived the same cause; the pitfalls in @sec-verification-fallacies-pitfalls show both failing together. A shared cause that the ledger does not name cannot be enumerated this way, which is why the forward analysis of the physical machine remains a separate source of faults.

The fault list now holds inverted design claims, forward-derived physical fault classes, the four authority cases, and compound faults drawn from named shared causes. It says what to inject but not where an injection is real, and that choice decides what each trial can prove.

## The Qualification Ladder {#sec-verification-qualification-ladder}

A simulator can stall the proposer of F1 at every sampled speed and payload overnight, but it cannot sag the drive bus of F4, because the simulated bus has no converter to lock out and no microcontroller to reset. This is the digital twin delusion again, now in its engineering form: the belief that millions of passing virtual rollout assertions (`assert clearance >= 0`) in a physics engine establish safety on the embodied machine.

The gap depends on what the simulator represents. A physics simulation that omits target execution and electrical dynamics can make the following idealizations; each must be checked against the claim under test:

1. **Computation takes zero virtual time:** The simulator pauses the simulation clock while the policy executes, treating heavy neural forward passes as instantaneous and decoupling inference latency from physical velocity ($d = v \tau_{\text{delay}}$).
2. **Memory bandwidth is infinite:** Tensors pass across shared in-memory references, omitting the shared-memory contention, cache evictions, and DMA serialization stalls that characterize an edge SoC.
3. **Power rails are infinitely stiff:** Supplies are modeled as constant voltages ($V = \text{const}$), ignoring the source and harness resistance that sags the drive bus by $\Delta V = I R$ when drive current steps (@sec-body-power-integrity), the inductive spikes of fast current edges, and the brownout resets either can cause.
4. **Clocks are perfectly synchronized:** The simulation advances via a single discrete time-step ($\Delta t$), eliminating real-world clock drift, interrupt jitter, and transceiver races between the neural host and the safety microcontroller.
5. **Contact mechanics are simplified:** Contact solvers approximate Coulomb friction, with linearized friction cones or with soft and convex relaxations that permit small creep under static load [@todorov2014convex], and usually omit the difference between static and kinetic friction, tire slip dynamics, and brake-lining glazing under repeated stops.

Each qualification environment closes, breaks, or substitutes different links of the loop running from sensing through inference, buses, drives, and plant. Consequently, evaluation environments do not form a strict linear hierarchy: a higher rung cannot subsume a lower one. Each yields a distinct category of evidence while remaining fundamentally blind to the physical mechanisms outside its boundary (@fig-15-qualification-ladder).

::: {#dfn-verification-four-stage-qualification-ladder .callout-definition title="Four-stage qualification ladder"}

***Four-stage qualification ladder***\index{Four-stage qualification ladder!definition}\index{Qualification ladder!definition} is the structured progression of cyber-physical evaluation environments that closes, breaks, or substitutes specific arcs in the causal loop to balance combinatorial test throughput against physical and temporal execution fidelity. Its four stages are Software-in-the-Loop (SIL), Processor-in-the-Loop (PIL), Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL), and in-situ physical fault rigs.

1.  **Significance**: No single test environment can validate a physical AI system. Software simulators allow parallel combinatorial sweeps but omit target silicon bus contention and material wear; physical rigs expose authentic mechanics and electrical transients but cannot execute destructive fault sweeps at scale.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a cumulative testing staircase where higher rungs subsume lower ones, each qualification rung exercises a different, partly overlapping set of causal mechanisms while remaining blind to others.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Assuming that passing extensive Software-in-the-Loop (SIL) simulation implies safety on embedded hardware. SIL abstracts away microcontroller clock drift, DMA bus lockups, interrupt jitter, and power supply voltage sag.

:::

### Causal loop fidelity across the four rungs {#sec-verification-qualification-rungs}

@Tbl-15-qualification-ladder gives each rung's substrate, the faults it can inject, its throughput, and where its evidence ends. For the mobile manipulator, software-in-the-loop\index{Software-in-the-loop} evidence ends at the plant model, where a brake modeled as a first-order lag has no lining temperature, tire slip, or torque limit. Processor-in-the-loop\index{Processor-in-the-loop} adds the cross-compiled binary on target silicon and so tests quantization and stack headroom; hardware-in-the-loop\index{Hardware-in-the-loop} benches put the two-processor implementation of @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning, its fieldbus, supplies, and drive stages against an FPGA plant or a dynamometer; and physical fault rigs\index{In-situ physical fault rigs} add the production base, brakes, harness, and floor. Two sources beside the ladder open the loop altogether. Trace replay keeps real sensor noise but supplies the frames that followed the original command rather than the new one. Shadow operation runs the candidate beside an incumbent controller, so if the candidate proposes a velocity that would carry the base past a rack end, its log records the command while the incumbent keeps the base where it belongs. Neither shows the physical consequence of a command.

A shadow deployment cannot let a stalled proposer drive the base toward a rack end that may hold a person, a simulator cannot reveal a race in transceiver silicon, and a hardware bench cannot run the millions of randomized runs that tail statistics need. Each fault injection therefore goes to the rung that exercises its causal mechanism.

::: {#fig-15-qualification-ladder fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative qualification trade-off**: Schematic throughput and fidelity coordinates, not measured benchmarks, place four environments from roughly $10^6$ software-only runs a day at zero hardware realism down to a handful of in-situ physical fault injections at full realism. The ladder is not a progression toward accuracy but a sequence of different blind spots, because each stage establishes evidence only within its own causal loop and stays blind to every mechanism outside it." fig-alt="Four-stage qualification ladder schematic charting throughput (runs per day, logarithmic from 10^6 down to 10^0) against hardware fidelity (0 to 100 percent). Four semantic stages descending along the Pareto trade-off: Software-in-the-Loop (SIL, cloud cluster, high throughput), Processor-in-the-Loop (PIL, target silicon), Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL, dyno testbed), and In-Situ (physical fault rig, field plant). Attribution: Original textbook graphic, CC BY 4.0."}
![](images/svg/fig15_qualification_ladder.svg){width="95%"}
:::

The choice of rung follows the failed premise. F1 needs target execution to test lease expiry under processor interference; F4 needs the production supply path and independent rail measurements. A stopping-distance claim also needs the loaded body and qualified floor. We can use simulation to select challenging conditions, then reproduce those conditions on the rung that contains the mechanism under test. Agreement between rungs supports only the mechanisms represented in both; the table records the remaining limits.

| Qualification Rung & Substrate                                     | Causal Loop Realism (Compute, Bus, Actuator, Plant)                                                                                                          | Fault Injection Mechanism & Scope                                                          | Throughput & Sample Scaling                                         | Physical & Temporal Fidelity                                                            | Primary Test Oracle & Evidentiary Limit                                                                                                                                                  |
|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Software-in-the-Loop (SIL)** (Host Workstation / Cloud Cluster)  | **Compute:** Synthetic / Host x86; **Bus:** Idealized zero-copy buffer; **Actuator:** Linear / saturation model; **Plant:** Numerical ODE/PDE solver         | Tensor bit-flips, synthetic sensor dropout, floor-friction, payload, and latency sweeps    | Parallel sweeps; throughput depends on model and compute allocation | High mathematical flexibility; zero target silicon, bus timing, or electrical realism   | **Oracle:** Mathematical assertion corridors and state invariants. **Limit:** Cannot validate target execution timing or unmodeled physical dynamics.                                    |
| **Processor-in-the-Loop (PIL)** (Target SoC / MCU Core Emulation)  | **Compute:** Real target silicon (ARM/RISC-V); **Bus:** Simulated bus interconnect; **Actuator:** Emulated command register; **Plant:** Real-time host model | Instruction cache evictions, register corruption via JTAG/BIST, interrupt jitter injection | Bound by target execution and cross-platform synchronization        | Instruction-set and compiler accurate; abstracts analog bus lines and actuator back-EMF | **Oracle:** Target register state, numerical equivalence, and execution-time profiles. **Limit:** Ignores physical transceiver bus contention, voltage droop, and thermal rise.          |
| **Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL)** (Target ECUs + Real-Time Plant Rig) | **Compute:** Production ECU / NPU; **Bus:** Real physical CAN/Ethernet; **Actuator:** Real motor drives / dyno; **Plant:** Hard real-time FPGA plant rig     | Pin break/short, CAN frame stuffing / babbling idiot, supply rail droop, load steps        | $1.0\times$ strict real-time ($24\text{ h/day}$ wall-clock limit)   | High electrical, timing, and protocol fidelity; bounded by FPGA plant model accuracy    | **Oracle:** Protocol CRC, bus deadline monitors, and interlock timings. **Limit:** Cannot execute destructive physical overload or simulate tire and lining wear.                        |
| **Physical Fault Rig** (Dynamometer Cell / Field Plant)            | **Compute:** Production ECU / NPU; **Bus:** Production harness & sensors; **Actuator:** Real physical mechanisms; **Plant:** Real base, arm, and floor       | Wheel clamps, magnetic brake stall, thermal heating, transducer bias drift                 | Wall-clock execution; constrained by wear and thermal reset         | Full authentic physics (Coulomb friction, wheel slip, thermal dissipation, wear)        | **Oracle:** Independent physical containment instrumentation and yield transducers. **Limit:** High financial cost per trial; destructive tests cannot scale to statistical tail bounds. |

: **The four-stage qualification ladder across cyber-physical boundaries**: The four qualification environments compared by computing substrate, exercised causal-loop elements, fault injection primitives, execution throughput, physical and temporal fidelity, and test oracle. {#tbl-15-qualification-ladder tbl-colwidths="[16,22,16,14,16,16]"}

::: {#fig-15-hil-avionics-testbed fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Hardware-in-the-loop testbed layout**: An illustrative integration layout places distributed controllers, wiring, power distribution, and fault-injection interfaces on an accessible rig. A warehouse-machine qualification fixture must reproduce the relevant production paths and independently measure the injected disturbance; the image does not document such a qualification." fig-alt="Full-scale distributed hardware-in-the-loop testbed showing production electronic control units, heavy-gauge wire harnesses, power distribution units, and programmable fault injection breakout interfaces mounted along an instrumented structural frame."}
![](images/jpg/fig15_real_hil_avionics_testbed_annotated.jpg){width="95%"}
:::

### The causal loop coverage rule and evidentiary limits {#sec-verification-qualification-limits}

The fidelity boundary of a test environment is where a model, an emulated bus, or a replayed trace severs the exchange of energy and information between computation and mechanics (@sec-boundary-causal-boundary). As illustrated by the testbed layout in @fig-15-hil-avionics-testbed, physical wire harnesses, ground returns, and distributed actuator units cannot be replaced by idealized desktop simulations without omitting inductive voltage droop, transmission reflections, and EMI coupling. No qualification rung can certify properties outside its causal boundary. SIL falsifies algorithmic logic. PIL falsifies numerical and compiler equivalence on the target and profiles execution, but it exchanges I/O over a debug or serial link, so timing under real I/O needs HIL. HIL falsifies bus contention, I/O timing, and electrical transients, and physical rigs falsify contact mechanics and thermal dissipation.

A higher rung therefore does not subsume or obsolete the lower ones. Test engineering is an optimization problem under resource constraints: parallel SIL can explore many combinations of lighting and obstacle conditions, whereas physical rigs exercise actual contact mechanics and require reset, inspection, and thermal recovery between trials. Each stage occupies a unique point on the Pareto frontier balancing combinatorial test throughput against physical causal fidelity. A mechanism the model omits cannot fail in it. A joint with unmodeled Coulomb breakaway friction and stator lag sits still for a dead time the simulator never shows and then trails the simulated trajectory, an instance of the omitted-mechanism class of @sec-training-sim-to-real-gap that only a rung with the real joint can expose.

### Scope of a formal verification result {#sec-verification-formal-limits}

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-nn-scale
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NEURAL-NETWORK VERIFICATION SCALE AGAINST THE RUNNING MACHINE'S PROPOSER (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-verification-formal-limits, @tbl-15-verification-state-of-practice.
# │ Goal: Compare the largest network scored in VNN-COMP 2025 with the running
# │       machine's intent model, to motivate verifying the permission path.
# │ Show: 138 million parameters; the 7B proposer is about 51x larger.
# │ How: ratio of parameter counts.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Embodied
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_params, fmt_multiple, check

class NNVerificationScale:
    """Scale of complete NN verification (as of 2025) against the machine's proposer."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    proposer_params = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator.intent_model.parameters  # category: datasheet
    # Largest scored network in VNN-COMP 2025 (VGGNet16 benchmark), @kaulen2025vnncomp; category: sourced
    vnn_max_params = 138e6 * ureg.param

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    ratio = float((proposer_params / vnn_max_params).to("dimensionless").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(ratio > 10, "The proposer must exceed the largest verified benchmark by more than an order of magnitude.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    vnn_max_params_str = fmt_params(vnn_max_params, precision=0)
    proposer_params_str = fmt_params(proposer_params, precision=0)
    ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(ratio), precision=0)  # displayed as "about"
```

A proof for the permission mechanism can establish a property over its modeled states and disturbances. Its application to the machine still depends on the plant model, observations, execution deadlines, and available actuation. The question for this machine is which component a proof can reach, and the state of neural-network verification answers it.

A neural-network verifier checks an **open-loop property**\index{Neural network verification!open-loop property}: for every input in a specified set, such as all images within a small perturbation of a nominal frame, the network's output satisfies a specified condition. Two mechanisms do the work. **Bound propagation**\index{Bound propagation} pushes the input set through the network layer by layer, replacing each nonlinear activation with linear upper and lower bounds, and returns a sound but possibly loose enclosure of the outputs; if the enclosure already satisfies the condition, the property holds. When it does not, **branch and bound**\index{Branch and bound!neural network verification} splits an unstable activation into its two linear pieces and bounds each half again, so the search is complete in principle and exponential in the number of splits in the worst case. Reluplex [@katz2017reluplex] and its successor Marabou [@wu2024marabou] reach completeness through a constraint solver instead; the α,β-CROWN verifier combines GPU-accelerated bound propagation with branch and bound [@xu2021alphacrown; @wang2021betacrown].

A **closed-loop property**\index{Neural network verification!closed-loop property} is a different object. It asks whether the state of a plant driven by a network controller stays inside a safe set over a horizon, so the verifier must compose the network's output bounds with the plant dynamics at every step and control the growth of the reachable set. Tools such as NNV, Verisig, and POLAR do this for small controllers and low-dimensional plants [@tran2020nnv; @ivanov2019verisig; @huang2022polar]. None of them takes camera frames as input: their state is the plant's few physical variables, which is exactly the form of the permission path's inputs and not the form of a vision-language-action policy's.

@Tbl-15-verification-state-of-practice dates the scale at which these tools operate. The largest network in the 2025 international verification competition had `{python} NNVerificationScale.vnn_max_params_str` parameters, and most scored benchmarks were far smaller [@kaulen2025vnncomp]. The running machine's `{python} NNVerificationScale.proposer_params_str`-parameter chunk policy is about `{python} NNVerificationScale.ratio_mult_str` larger than that outlier, takes a stream of images rather than a bounded input set, and has no specification of the form "for all inputs in this set" that would mean anything at the rack end. Complete verification of the proposer is therefore out of reach, and the obstacle is the missing specification as much as the scale. That is the argument for the architecture this book has built since @sec-boundary: the learned proposer is evaluated, while the small permission path, whose inputs are a handful of physical quantities and whose property is a stopping invariant, is the part a proof can reach.

| Method class                       | Representative tool                                                       | What a result establishes                                                                    | Scale and limit, as of 2026                                                                                                                                             |
|:-----------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Complete open-loop NN verification | α,β-CROWN [@wang2021betacrown]; Marabou 2.0 [@wu2024marabou]              | A property holds for every input in a bounded set, or a counterexample input                 | α,β-CROWN ranked first in each competition from 2021 to 2025; scored benchmarks reach `{python} NNVerificationScale.vnn_max_params_str` parameters [@kaulen2025vnncomp] |
| Closed-loop reachability           | NNV [@tran2020nnv]; Verisig [@ivanov2019verisig]; POLAR [@huang2022polar] | The plant state under a network controller stays in a safe set over a horizon                | Small controllers and low-dimensional plants; sets grow conservative over long horizons                                                                                 |
| STL falsification                  | S-TaLiRo [@annpureddy2011staliro]; Breach [@donze2010breach]              | A counterexample trajectory with negative robustness, or none found within the search budget | Black-box simulation of any model; no certificate from an unsuccessful search                                                                                           |
| Rare-event estimation              | Importance sampling with the cross-entropy method [@okelly2018scalable]   | A failure probability under a declared operational distribution, with its variance           | Only as good as the declared distribution and the proposal's coverage of the failure set                                                                                |

: **Verification methods and their reach, as of 2026**: Representative tools for each method class, what a result establishes, and the scale at which it currently operates. The mechanisms in the prose are durable; the named tools and scales will change, so the table carries its date. {#tbl-15-verification-state-of-practice tbl-colwidths="[20,24,28,28]"}

High-dimensional reachability, nonlinear contact, and hybrid switching can make analysis of the permission path itself expensive or conservative. Those limits do not make every useful proof impossible. They favor a smaller, explicit permission claim whose premises can be challenged independently on the target hardware.

To prevent false confidence, every reported verification result must explicitly state which elements of the causal loop were physically real, which were simulated, which were replayed from static logs, which were bypassed, and which remained unobserved. A claim that the permission path stopped the base within `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_str` means nothing without specifying whether the wheel-speed signal was generated by a differential equation, read from a physical encoder over the real fieldbus, or replayed from a digital buffer. Specifying this causal mapping exposes the assumptions underlying each test, so that unmodeled physics cannot hide a latent hazard.

## Fault Injection on Hardware {#sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection}

A fault injected in simulation tests the modeled response. Unless explicitly represented and validated, clock drift, shared-memory interference, scheduling jitter, and electrical transients remain outside that evidence. On the machine, contention on a shared bus, clock drift between microcontrollers, DMA stalls, and voltage drop across inductive drivers decide whether an intervention executes in time. On an embodied machine, fault injection must therefore pass through the compute, communication, and power substrate. Injection happens on target hardware, through the real transceivers, timers, shared buses, and enforcement path, while an independent containment rig protects the test facility.

**In-situ fault injection**\index{In-situ fault injection!definition} is the deliberate, deterministic introduction of physical, electrical, and computational disturbances (including sensor register latches, clock drift, bus contention, supply brownouts, and actuator load stalls) directly into target production silicon and mechanics while operating under authentic electrical, thermal, and dynamic loads.

### Physical injection needles across sensor, bus, and power {#sec-verification-injection-needles}

A fault injected in software above the driver never exercises the interface where the physical fault enters, so a campaign places its injectors at the physical interfaces themselves.[^fn-hw-hil-needles] Four kinds cover the machine's claims:

[^fn-hw-hil-needles]: **Injection fixtures**\index{Fault injection!circuitry schematics}: Power injectors switch or program the supply with solid-state devices, and bus injectors drive the lines through high-impedance buffers. The instrumentation must be isolated from the drive's high-current transients, or the witness fails with the machine. The achievable edge rate and isolation are properties of the specific fixture and belong in the trial record.

1. *Sensor ingress injectors:* inline interposers on the camera's serial link freeze frames, delay them with their capture stamps preserved, or corrupt pixel data at the physical boundary without modifying software drivers.
2. *Fieldbus disturbance nodes:* CAN-FD and EtherCAT disturbance nodes corrupt checksums, force bit collisions that drive a node into its bus-off state, drop synchronization frames, and emulate a babbling idiot, a faulty node that transmits continuously and starves the others of bus time.
3. *Supply injectors:* a programmable supply standing in for the pack, together with an electronic load, steps the drive bus and the logic rails through declared waveforms. The delivered waveform is measured, because a fixture's slew-rate limit bounds which transients a trial can reproduce.
4. *Dynamometer actuator injectors:* load machines coupled to wheel hubs or arm joints command step torques that emulate bearing seizures, brake-lining glazing, or abrupt mechanical jams while the motor current response is measured.

### Timing faults across clock domains {#sec-verification-hardware-timing-search}

Camera capture, proposal generation, permission ticks, and fieldbus cycles run on different clocks. A reproducible test records the disturbance's phase relative to each relevant event. Sweeping those phases challenges races that an injection at one fixed phase cannot reach; searching them does not establish that the worst case has been found.

Consider F2 on the hardware. The navigation camera stamps each frame at capture, and the frame's age at dispatch is budgeted at `{python} RackEndVerification.t_age_str` (@sec-perception-transduction-calibration). At `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` the base covers `{python} RackEndVerification.per_ms_str` in every millisecond, so an unaccounted delay spends the reserve directly. The `{python} RackEndVerification.upper_age_str` upper-age value applies at dispatch; the evidence continues aging during admission and execution. A per-tick test must use the remaining stopping budget and the active command's validity, not reset age at dispatch or reuse that dispatch threshold as a universal live limit. Left undetected for `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str`, it consumes all `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str`. Neither the camera's datasheet readout time nor the timestamp on a single frame establishes how quickly the permission path notices. A measured $P_{99}$ detection time leaves the worst case unbounded (@sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses), so the containment claim needs a detection bound justified over the declared compute-load, bus-load, and thermal envelope.

Testing the two-processor implementation\index{Two-processor implementation!fault injection} (@sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning) demands physical fault injection at the boundaries its claims name. @Tbl-15-fault-classification gives each case's detector, response, and pass condition; the list adds how each fault is injected and, where it matters, where its events are timed:

- **Stale Observation Injection (F2):** An inline FPGA interceptor latches a navigation-camera frame at the image signal processor, or suppresses encoder updates, while preserving the original hardware timestamp. Detector assertion, powered deceleration onset, and wheel speed are measured on independent instruments.
- **Expired Lease Revocation (F1):** The test framework lets the proposer renew once and then suppresses every later renewal. Lease expiry, revocation on the enforcer's next `{python} RackEndVerification.t_tick_str` tick, and powered deceleration onset are each measured on their own wire and clock.
- **Lost-Frame Injection (F3):** A fieldbus disturbance node drops or corrupts EtherCAT frames at a drive's slave port while the base cruises. Each lost `{python} RackEndVerification.t_bus_str` cycle costs `{python} RackEndVerification.per_ms_str` of travel at the aisle speed.
- **Drive-Bus Droop and Feed-Loss Injection (F4a, F4b):** A programmable supply standing in for the pack at its `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_low_str` depleted point carries the `{python} RackEndVerification.i_rail_str` transient of hard drive acceleration with the application SoC at full load, then steps the drive bus below the `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_uvlo_str` converter lockout, because the load alone leaves `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_margin_str` of headroom (@sec-body-power-integrity), while the permission path runs on the isolated, held-up rail that @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder sizes and the placement record carries (@sec-placement-hardware-allocation). An independent digitizer records the permission-path heartbeat, and powered deceleration onset is timed from the undervoltage flag. F4b opens the permission rail's feed during the longest stop the enforcer can admit on an inspected floor, the resident stop from its `{python} RackEndVerification.ceiling_insp_str` ceiling. Independent measurements must also establish surviving drive authority and energy absorption throughout the powered stop. Logic hold-up alone leaves that premise open. A reset of the permission path is `FAIL` in either trial, whatever the stopping distance, because a stop that power loss hands to the spring brakes mid-motion is not the stop the claim budgets.
- **Duplicate Writer Injection (A1):** A second bus master writes a base-drive channel, either as a frame under the enforcer's EtherCAT identifier or as a DMA write to the drive's command register, while the policy and a remote assistant both command.
- **Tier Bypass Injection (A2):** The testbed submits a policy proposal while `MAN` is active and, in a separate trial, a remote-assistant command that opposes the enforcer's admitted limit.
- **Handover Stall Injection (A3):** The testbed freezes the remote assistant's input during `PEND` and drops the acknowledgment frames at both speeds, and both fallback dispatch and physical onset at the drive are timed independently. The waiting allowance bounds dispatch; onset must also satisfy the allocated command-to-response interval.
- **Replay and Forgery Injection (A4):** The testbed replays a captured `veto_path`, `manual_drive`, or `accept_item` packet and sends another with a corrupted authentication tag.

::: {#fig-15-hardware-fault-injection fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative multi-channel fault trace**: Hypothetical sensor, lease, monitor, drive, and torque signals demonstrate the separate events a test must witness. The plotted timings and torque values are schematic assumptions, not an experiment or the running machine's F1 bounds. A monitor flag alone does not establish the physical response." fig-alt="Oscilloscope-style multi-signal trace showing five tracks across 50 milliseconds: ADC Sensor freezing at 20 ms, Intent Lease dropping at 20 ms, Safety NMI asserting at 24 ms, Permission/Drive switching to safe takeover at 26 ms, and Actuator Torque peaking at 162 N·m below the 165 N·m red dashed limit before coming to rest at 43 ms before the 45 ms deadline."}
![](images/svg/fig15_hardware_fault_injection.svg){width="95%"}
:::

The hypothetical traces in @fig-15-hardware-fault-injection illustrate why the sensor, lease, monitor, drive, and physical response need separate channels. They are not measurements from the running machine and do not use its F1 timing contract. A real trace must establish the same causal sequence using the machine's precommitted bounds and independent witnesses.

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-clock-drift
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLOCK-CONVERSION DRIFT AGAINST THE F2 BOUND (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: hardware fault-injection section, @eq-verification-clock-drift.
# │ Goal: Show how quickly oscillator drift between the application processor
# │       and the safety microcontroller spends the 0.2 ms clock-conversion
# │       bound that F2's refusal threshold rests on, and what a sync blackout costs.
# │ Show: 200 ppm worst relative rate; bound consumed after 1 s unsynchronized;
# │       20 us per 100 ms sync period; 80 us over a four-period blackout, 95 us
# │       with one sigma of jitter; 100 us after a fifth missed period.
# │ How: drift = rate x elapsed time; allowance = RackEndVerification.eps_sync.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import microsecond, millisecond, second
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_latency, check

class ClockDriftVerification:
    """Oscillator drift between the two processors, tested against the clock-conversion bound."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    ppm_ap = 100  # application-processor oscillator limit, ppm; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    ppm_mcu = 50  # safety-microcontroller oscillator limit, ppm; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    ppm_thermal = 50  # separately bounded thermal contribution, ppm; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    t_sync = 100 * millisecond  # healthy sync period; scenario assumption; category: chosen
    n_blackout = 4  # sync periods between two good frames (three dropped); scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    sigma_jitter = 15 * microsecond  # observed sync jitter, one standard deviation; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    eps_sync = RackEndVerification.eps_sync  # clock-conversion bound of the observation contract; category: derived

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    ppm_total = ppm_ap + ppm_mcu + ppm_thermal
    rate = ppm_total * microsecond / second  # worst relative drift rate
    t_consume = (eps_sync / rate).to(second)
    drift_period = (rate * t_sync).to(microsecond)
    t_blackout = (n_blackout * t_sync).to(millisecond)
    drift_blackout = (rate * t_blackout).to(microsecond)
    one_sigma = (drift_blackout + sigma_jitter).to(microsecond)
    drift_fifth = (rate * (n_blackout + 1) * t_sync).to(microsecond)
    fifth_share = float((drift_fifth / eps_sync).to("dimensionless").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(ppm_total == 200, "Worst relative rate must be 200 ppm.")
    check(abs(t_consume.magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Drift alone must consume the 0.2 ms bound after 1 s.")
    check(abs(drift_blackout.magnitude - 80.0) < 1e-9, "Four-period blackout must drift 80 us.")
    check(one_sigma < eps_sync.to(microsecond), "The one-sigma scenario must sit inside the conversion bound.")
    check(abs(fifth_share - 0.5) < 1e-9, "A fifth missed period must spend half the bound.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    ppm_ap_str = fmt_int(ppm_ap)
    ppm_mcu_str = fmt_int(ppm_mcu)
    ppm_thermal_str = fmt_int(ppm_thermal)
    ppm_total_str = fmt_int(ppm_total)
    t_consume_str = fmt_latency(t_consume, unit=second, precision=0)
    t_sync_str = fmt_latency(t_sync, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    drift_period_str = fmt_latency(drift_period, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_blackout_str = fmt_latency(t_blackout, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    drift_blackout_str = fmt_latency(drift_blackout, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    sigma_jitter_str = fmt_latency(sigma_jitter, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    one_sigma_str = fmt_latency(one_sigma, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    drift_fifth_str = fmt_latency(drift_fifth, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
```

### Distributed clock drift and synchronization blackouts {#sec-verification-clock-drift-sync}

Testing distributed loops exposes clock-conversion risk even when each processor meets its local schedule. F2's refusal threshold rests on the `{python} RackEndVerification.eps_sync_str` bound for converting a capture stamp to the safety microcontroller's clock, and that bound is itself a claim to test. Take illustrative oscillator limits of ±`{python} ClockDriftVerification.ppm_ap_str` ppm on the application processor and ±`{python} ClockDriftVerification.ppm_mcu_str` ppm on the safety microcontroller, plus a separately bounded `{python} ClockDriftVerification.ppm_thermal_str` ppm thermal contribution that those specifications do not include. The worst relative rate is then `{python} ClockDriftVerification.ppm_total_str` ppm, and drift alone would consume the `{python} RackEndVerification.eps_sync_str` bound after `{python} ClockDriftVerification.t_consume_str` without resynchronization. A healthy `{python} ClockDriftVerification.t_sync_str` sync period limits that drift contribution to `{python} ClockDriftVerification.drift_period_str`; network and conversion error must be budgeted separately.

Suppose two good sync frames arrive `{python} ClockDriftVerification.t_blackout_str` apart while the three scheduled frames between them are dropped. The blackout lasts four sync periods, and the bounded drift contribution grows to `{python} ClockDriftVerification.drift_blackout_str`. If the observed synchronization jitter has standard deviation $\sigma_{\text{jitter}}$ = `{python} ClockDriftVerification.sigma_jitter_str`, adding one sigma to the drift rate $r_{\text{drift}}$ times the blackout $T_{\text{blackout}}$ gives
$$\Delta t_{\text{one-sigma scenario}}=r_{\text{drift}}\,T_{\text{blackout}}+\sigma_{\text{jitter}}$$ {#eq-verification-clock-drift}
or `{python} ClockDriftVerification.one_sigma_str`. The one-sigma value in @eq-verification-clock-drift is not a hard bound; a deterministic deadline needs a justified jitter envelope and a clock-conversion test. A fifth elapsed period, with four intervening sync frames dropped, gives `{python} ClockDriftVerification.drift_fifth_str` of drift alone, before jitter, half the `{python} RackEndVerification.eps_sync_str` bound on which F2's threshold rests. If clock drift and synchronization jitter combine to breach that bound, two symmetric physical failure modes jeopardize the machine. On one hand, a completely fresh camera frame may appear artificially aged when evaluated against the safety microcontroller's drifted clock, causing the enforcer to falsely reject valid proposals and trip an unprompted emergency stop, stranding the base in an active warehouse aisle. On the other hand, a dangerously delayed observation may appear falsely fresh, duping the permission path into executing proposals computed from obsolete obstacle coordinates while the loaded base cruises at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` toward a closed aisle gate.

Every injection on the hardware ends with the same obligation. The detector that fired, the moment of refusal, the takeover at the drive, and the physical outcome are measured on instruments the fault cannot reach, on one reference clock, and a trial that loses any of them has not shown what it set out to show. The hardware campaign therefore produces records rather than a pass count, each binding one trial to its claim, its envelope point, its builds, and its evidence.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Hardware-in-the-loop stress results furnish the evidentiary warrants for safety cases in @sec-release-safety-cases-claims.
:::

## Searching Beyond the First Trial {#sec-verification-search-campaign}

The F1 specification establishes a reproducible question, witness, and verdict rule. Finding less obvious failures requires varying the conditions and measuring how close each run comes to its limits. These searches prioritize tests; they do not replace the coverage record.

### Signal temporal logic and quantitative robustness {#sec-verification-stl-robustness}

**Signal Temporal Logic (STL)** combines physical predicates with real-time conditions such as always remaining within a distance bound or eventually stopping before a deadline [@maler2004monitoring] (@sec-appendix-ml-stl). These requirements admit **quantitative robustness semantics**\index{Quantitative robustness semantics!definition} [@fainekos2009robustness]. Instead of a simple binary pass/fail boolean flag, robustness is a continuous real-valued metric $\rho(\phi, s, t) \in \mathbb{R}$ that measures *how far* a real-valued signal trajectory $s: \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ remains from violating or satisfying a temporal requirement $\phi$ at time $t$.

For an atomic physical predicate $\pi \equiv (f(s(t)) \ge 0)$ (such as spatial clearance $d(t) - d_{\text{safe}} \ge 0$), quantitative robustness evaluates the signed predicate margin: $\rho(\pi, s, t) = f(s(t))$. Across temporal horizons, safety invariants evaluate worst-case (minimum) margin, while eventual deadlines evaluate the best-case (maximum):
$$\rho(\square_{[0, T]} \phi, s, 0) = \min_{t \in [0, T]} \rho(\phi, s, t), \qquad \rho(\lozenge_{[0, \tau]} \phi, s, 0) = \max_{t \in [0, \tau]} \rho(\phi, s, t).$$ {#eq-verification-stl-recursive-robustness}[^fn-math-stl-semantics]
Here $\square_{[0,T]}$ reads "always on $[0,T]$" and $\lozenge_{[0,\tau]}$ reads "eventually within $\tau$."

[^fn-math-stl-semantics]: **Signal Temporal Logic Quantitative Semantics**\index{Signal Temporal Logic!recursive semantics}: In Signal Temporal Logic, quantitative robustness $\rho(\phi, s, t)$ maps continuous signal trajectories to signed real margins: $\rho(\neg \phi, s, t) = -\rho(\phi, s, t)$, $\rho(\phi_1 \land \phi_2, s, t) = \min(\rho(\phi_1, s, t), \rho(\phi_2, s, t))$, and $\rho(\phi_1 \lor \phi_2, s, t) = \max(\rho(\phi_1, s, t), \rho(\phi_2, s, t))$. For the bounded until operator, $\rho(\phi_1 \mathcal{U}_{[a, b]} \phi_2, s, t) = \max_{t' \in [t+a, t+b]} \min(\rho(\phi_2, s, t'), \min_{t'' \in [t, t']} \rho(\phi_1, s, t''))$.

The sign and magnitude of $\rho$ in @eq-verification-stl-recursive-robustness establish an immediate operational interpretation:
$$\rho > 0 \implies \text{satisfied with positive margin } \rho, \qquad \rho < 0 \implies \text{violated with shortfall depth } |\rho|.$$
For example, if the clearance margin is $\rho = +0.15\,\text{m}$, the minimum clearance along the trajectory exceeded the required clearance by 15 centimeters; if $\rho = -0.04\,\text{m}$, the machine breached the specified clearance by 4 centimeters, and whether contact occurred depends on how that clearance was defined.[^fn-math-stl-robustness]

This value margin is **space robustness**\index{Space robustness}: how far the signal's value could move before the verdict changes. It does not measure lateness. A deadline violation is a margin in time, and **time robustness**\index{Time robustness} is a separate semantics that asks how far the signal could shift in time before the verdict changes [@donze2010robust]. The two answer different questions and should not be mixed inside one formula. For F1 the simplest correct treatment keeps the onset deadline outside the STL formula, as a scalar predicate on the measured onset time, and scores the distance requirement with space robustness.

[^fn-math-stl-robustness]: **Quantitative Robustness Semantics**\index{Quantitative robustness semantics!intuition}: Each predicate has a signed margin in its own physical unit: clearance may use meters, powered deceleration onset milliseconds, and contact force newtons. A negative margin falsifies that predicate. A minimum across unlike units is meaningless; a combined dimensionless STL score requires each margin to be divided by a predeclared positive scale of the same unit. The record retains raw margins and scales so a pass or failure remains physically interpretable.

The F1 oracle therefore has two parts. Powered deceleration must begin within `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` of the last successful lease renewal, and travel from that same event must remain within `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_aisle_stop_bound_str` at the aisle speed, a space-robustness predicate on position. A different reference event requires a different distance bound.

For a numerical illustration, take one F1 trace at the aisle speed whose powered deceleration onset comes `{python} RackEndVerification.late_onset_str` late, at `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_late_str` after the last valid renewal. The onset margin against the `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` bound is `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_onset_str`. The base covers `{python} RackEndVerification.late_extra_str` more before braking begins, so travel from renewal to rest reaches `{python} RackEndVerification.travel_late_str` and the distance margin against the `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_aisle_stop_bound_str` oracle is `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_dist_str`. Both predicates fail, and the record reports both in their own units. Combining them into one score with `min` requires the declared scales of the footnote above. With scales chosen equal to the bounds themselves, the normalized margins are `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_onset_n_str` for onset and `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_dist_n_str` for distance, so the onset predicate sets the combined score. A different choice of scales would change which predicate dominates, which is why the scales are fixed before the trial. These values are model arithmetic on a stipulated trace, not measurements.

Robustness transforms verification into **temporal logic falsification as adversarial optimization**\index{Temporal logic falsification!definition}. In classical machine learning, adversarial attacks (such as FGSM or PGD) search for an input perturbation $\delta$ within an $\epsilon$-ball ($\|\delta\|_\infty \le \epsilon$) that maximizes task loss: $\max_{\|\delta\|_\infty \le \epsilon} \mathcal{L}(f(x + \delta), y)$. In cyber-physical verification, temporal logic falsification is the continuous dynamic equivalent: rather than perturbing static feature vectors, an adversarial optimizer searches over initial condition spaces and time-varying physical disturbance trajectories within a bounded physical disturbance budget to minimize quantitative STL robustness. The robustness score acts directly as the adversarial falsification loss.

Uniform random sampling of a high-dimensional state space requires an intractable number of trials to observe a rare corner-case collision; an adversarial falsification engine searches actively for the disturbance sequences that drive the system closest to invariant violation.

### Formulating falsification as trajectory optimization {#sec-verification-falsification-trajectory-formulation}

Formally, let $\theta_0 \in \Theta_0$ represent the machine's initial state vector (speed, payload, heading, battery state-of-charge), and let $w(t) \in \mathcal{W}$ denote an adversarial disturbance trajectory spanning the test horizon $[0, T]$. In physical systems, $w(t)$ cannot be an unconstrained discontinuous function: physical actuators, sensors, and environmental states have finite bandwidth and inertia. We therefore parameterize disturbance trajectories over a compact parameter space $\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}$ using smooth basis functions (such as B-splines, cubic splines, or Fourier series):
$$w(t; \mathbf{p}) = \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbf{p}_k B_k(t)$$
where $B_k(t)$ are time-dependent basis functions and $\mathbf{p}_k$ are bounded coefficients.

The temporal logic falsification problem is formulated as finding the worst-case parameter combination that minimizes quantitative robustness:
$$\min_{\theta_0 \in \Theta_0, \, \mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}} \rho(\phi, s(\theta_0, w(\mathbf{p})), 0) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|w(t; \mathbf{p})\|_\infty \le \Delta_w, \quad \forall t \in [0, T].$$ {#eq-verification-adversarial-falsification}

The disturbance budget $\Delta_w$ in @eq-verification-adversarial-falsification constrains the magnitude of the optical, acoustic, contact, and execution disturbances already derived from the envelope. Magnitude alone does not make a trajectory realizable. The basis, coefficient bounds, and test fixture must also represent its rate of change and duration. A programmable load that cannot reproduce a simulated voltage transient leaves that counterexample untested on hardware.

The campaign therefore retains both the requested disturbance and its independently measured realization. If the fixture fails to deliver the precommitted disturbance, the trial is invalid for that test even if the machine stops. A realizable counterexample can reject the stated claim; a successful search over a restricted parameterization still leaves disturbances outside that parameterization open.

### Selecting a search method {#sec-verification-optimization-engines}

Contact transitions and discrete controller states can make the robustness objective nonsmooth, so derivative-free methods are useful. Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) adapts a distribution over disturbance parameters and can explore correlated changes in speed, friction, and timing. Bayesian optimization uses a surrogate and its uncertainty to select additional trials when physical runs are expensive. Neither method guarantees a global minimum from a finite campaign. The record retains search bounds, seeds, evaluated cases, and fixture constraints so that another engineer can identify what was actually challenged.

Two established toolboxes package this loop for models of cyber-physical systems. S-TaLiRo [@annpureddy2011staliro] and Breach [@donze2010breach] take an STL requirement and a simulation model, compute robustness on each simulated trace, and drive a stochastic or local optimizer toward negative robustness. A related family treats the disturbance sequence itself as the decision variable. **Adaptive stress testing**\index{Adaptive stress testing} [@lee2020adaptive] searches the disturbance sequence with Monte Carlo tree search or reinforcement learning for the most likely path to failure, not merely any path, which ranks counterexamples by how plausible their disturbances are. A survey of these black-box methods organizes them by what each returns: a counterexample, the most likely failure, or a failure probability [@corso2021survey]. Only the last of these is an estimate of operational risk, and @sec-verification-importance-sampling shows what it takes.

A simulated minimum margin still has to survive the difference between the simulator and the machine; @sec-verification-sim-to-real-bounds derives the discount it must cover. Passing that check on searched trajectories does not prove a global minimum or cover disturbances the search did not visit.

The proof-scope limits of @sec-verification-formal-limits also apply here. An open-loop network certificate concerns a specified input-output property. Connecting it to a stopping claim requires the plant, timing, and sensing premises of the closed loop. Search challenges those premises and can return a counterexample; exhaustion of its trial budget supplies no certificate of their universal validity.

::: {#chk-verification-temporal-logic-oracles-and-falsification .callout-checkpoint title="Temporal logic oracles and test precommitment"}

Before executing automated falsification against physical AI policies, verify your understanding of temporal logic specifications and test validity criteria:

- [ ] **Quantitative robustness interpretation**: Can you explain how Signal Temporal Logic replaces binary pass/fail assertions with a signed predicate margin, and how its units and reference limit determine the meaning of a negative score?
- [ ] **Adversarial optimization of disturbance trajectories**: Can you describe how black-box optimizers leverage quantitative robustness scores to discover worst-case combinations of latency, noise, and friction?
- [ ] **Test invalidation vs. failure criteria**: Can you distinguish between an execution that falsifies a safety invariant and an invalid trial where testbed preconditions or fault injection mechanisms failed?
:::

Search returns candidate counterexamples and measured margins. When a candidate comes from simulation, using it in a physical claim requires an account of the discrepancy between the modeled and actual trajectories.

### Sim-to-real transfer validation and discrepancy bounds {#sec-verification-sim-to-real-bounds}

In physical AI systems, high-throughput simulation (SIL) is indispensable for exploring combinatorial corner cases, but relying on simulation assertions without bounding transfer error is the essence of the digital twin delusion: an unvalidated simulator is an engine of confirmation bias. To use simulation sweeps as valid evidentiary warrants in a structured safety case, the engineering team must formally validate and bound the **sim-to-real transfer gap** $\epsilon_{\text{gap}}$\index{Sim-to-real transfer gap!discrepancy bounds}\index{Simulation-to-reality leap!validation bounds}.

Let $s_{\text{sim}}(t; \theta, u) \in \mathcal{S}$ and $s_{\text{real}}(t; \theta, u) \in \mathcal{S}$ denote the system state trajectories in simulation and on target physical hardware under matched declared conditions $\theta$ (initial speed, payload, floor friction) and input history $u$. Replaying identical inputs establishes an open-loop comparison. A claim about the deployed policy instead requires a discrepancy bound for matched closed-loop trials, including the different commands that changed observations can induce; the input-replay bound alone cannot establish it. The continuous transfer discrepancy is the supremum error across the test horizon $[0, T]$ measured under a task-weighted physical norm:
$$\epsilon_{\text{gap}} = \sup_{t \in [0, T]} \|s_{\text{real}}(t) - s_{\text{sim}}(t)\|_W$$ {#eq-verification-sim2real-gap}
where $\|\cdot\|_W$ first divides position, velocity, and actuator torque errors by predeclared positive reference scales in meters, meters per second, and newton-meters, respectively, then applies dimensionless task weights. The record fixes those scales and weights; the resulting discrepancy is dimensionless, and $L_\phi$ has the units of the predicate margin.

The transfer calculation requires a bound that applies to the claimed trajectories, rather than only the largest discrepancy observed in a finite test. In plain terms, the allowable model error must be subtracted from the simulated margin. Consider an STL safety requirement $\phi$ whose atomic predicates $f(s(t)) \ge 0$ are Lipschitz continuous with Lipschitz constant $L_\phi = \sup_{s_1 \ne s_2} |f(s_1) - f(s_2)| / \|s_1 - s_2\|_W$. In plain terms, $L_\phi$ is the largest rate at which the margin can change per unit of state error; for a clearance predicate in meters and a norm that measures position error in meters, it is 1. By Lipschitz continuity, the physical predicate error is bounded pointwise by the state discrepancy:
$$|f(s_{\text{real}}(t)) - f(s_{\text{sim}}(t))| \le L_\phi \|s_{\text{real}}(t) - s_{\text{sim}}(t)\|_W \le L_\phi \epsilon_{\text{gap}}$$
which guarantees that at every instant $t \in [0, T]$:
$$f(s_{\text{real}}(t)) \ge f(s_{\text{sim}}(t)) - L_\phi \epsilon_{\text{gap}}.$$
Taking the infimum across the temporal horizon $t \in [0, T]$ for an invariance property $\phi \equiv \square_{[0, T]} (f(s(t)) \ge 0)$, the guaranteed lower bound on physical robustness in the real world is:
$$\rho_{\text{real}} \ge \rho_{\text{sim}} - L_\phi \epsilon_{\text{gap}}.$$ {#eq-verification-robustness-discount}
The term $L_\phi \epsilon_{\text{gap}}$ in @eq-verification-robustness-discount acts as an inescapable **sim-to-real robustness discount**. If simulated robustness $\rho_{\text{sim}}$ is smaller than $L_\phi \epsilon_{\text{gap}}$, the simulation pass provides zero physical safety guarantee: the real system can breach the safe invariant set ($\rho_{\text{real}} < 0$) even though every simulated trial returned a positive margin.

The rack-end claim makes the discount concrete. Score the distance predicate in meters and let the norm measure position error with a 1 m scale, a modeling choice that makes $L_\phi = 1$. Suppose a simulated stop ends with the whole `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str` reserve intact. The discount of @eq-verification-robustness-discount then leaves a positive physical margin only if $\epsilon_{\text{gap}} <$ `{python} RackEndVerification.eps_gap_max_str`, that is, only if the simulated and real trajectories never differ by as much as the reserve itself. A simulator whose stopping position is validated to within a few centimeters transfers most of the margin; one that has never been compared with a measured stop transfers none of it.

The coupled-boundary examples identify what this discount must cover: drivetrain lag changes delivered torque, contact conditions change braking traction, and target execution changes response time. A bound calibrated with an unloaded, cool machine cannot silently extend to a loaded, thermally throttled one. The record must state the conditions over which the discrepancy bound is justified and separate that bound from the largest error merely observed in the paired trials.

Empirical validation of $\epsilon_{\text{gap}}$ requires systematic paired benchmarking. The physical machine (or HIL dynamometer) executes calibrated excitation trajectories (step steer, chirp braking, load rejection) across the operating envelope, measuring state trajectories with independent ground-truth instrumentation (laser trackers, torque transducers). The empirical discrepancy $\hat{\epsilon}_{\text{gap}}$ is recorded with the fault records. If the transfer argument relies on domain randomization distributions $\mathcal{D}_{\text{DR}}$ covering physical hardware dispersion, it must justify the following inclusion over the claimed conditions; finite paired measurements can challenge the inclusion but cannot establish it globally:
$$\mathcal{S}_{\text{real}}(\theta) \subseteq \bigcup_{\tilde{\theta} \sim \mathcal{D}_{\text{DR}}} \mathcal{S}_{\text{sim}}(\tilde{\theta}).$$
If unmodeled physical effects—such as actuator latency, stator saturation, gear backlash, or Coulomb stiction—cause physical trajectories to escape the randomized simulation bundle, the sim-to-real transfer is unvalidated, and SIL test passes cannot serve as warrants in the release safety case.

## Interpreting Campaign Statistics {#sec-verification-campaign-statistics}

A list of adversarial trials is not yet an estimate of operational risk. The sampling procedure determines which population a statistic describes, and missing witnesses remain missing evidence in every analysis.

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-injected-population-trials
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ZERO-MISS INJECTION COUNTS FOR A SAMPLED FAULT POPULATION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: fault-manifest section and @nbk-verification-hardware-fault-injection-coverage-mean-time.
# │ Show: Zero-miss injections needed to put a one-sided upper limit on the miss probability.
# │ How: n = ceil(ln(1 - C) / ln(1 - p)), the zero-failure sizing of @sec-evaluation-trial-limits.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_zero_failure_sample_size
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_percent, fmt_int, check

class InjectedPopulationTrials:
    """Zero-miss injection counts for a declared fault population."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen
    p_miss_1 = 0.01  # target upper limit on miss probability; category: chosen
    p_miss_2 = 0.001  # tighter target upper limit; category: chosen
    # Component fault rates for the coverage notebook, in FIT (faults per 1e9 h)
    fit_sensors = 1500  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    fit_compute = 1000  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    fit_power = 2500  # transceivers and power management; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    fit_gate = 4800  # gate drivers; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    fit_target_1 = 100  # unmitigated-rate target; category: chosen
    fit_target_2 = 10  # tighter unmitigated-rate target; category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_1 = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(1.0 - p_miss_1, confidence=confidence)
    n_2 = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(1.0 - p_miss_2, confidence=confidence)
    fit_raw = fit_sensors + fit_compute + fit_power + fit_gate
    c_diag_1 = 1.0 - fit_target_1 / fit_raw  # required coverage: lambda_raw (1 - C) <= target
    c_diag_2 = 1.0 - fit_target_2 / fit_raw

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_1 == 299, "Unexpected zero-miss count for a 1 percent limit")
    check(n_2 == 2995, "Unexpected zero-miss count for a 0.1 percent limit")
    check(fit_raw == 9800, "Component fault rates must sum to 9,800 FIT")
    check(c_diag_1 < c_diag_2 < 1.0, "A tighter target must need more coverage")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    confidence_pct_str = fmt_percent(confidence, precision=0)
    p_miss_1_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_miss_1, precision=0)
    p_miss_2_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_miss_2, precision=1)
    n_1_str = fmt_int(n_1, commas=True)
    n_2_str = fmt_int(n_2, commas=True)
    fit_sensors_str = fmt_int(fit_sensors, commas=True)
    fit_compute_str = fmt_int(fit_compute, commas=True)
    fit_power_str = fmt_int(fit_power, commas=True)
    fit_gate_str = fmt_int(fit_gate, commas=True)
    fit_raw_str = fmt_int(fit_raw, commas=True)
    fit_target_1_str = fmt_int(fit_target_1)
    fit_target_2_str = fmt_int(fit_target_2)
    c_diag_1_pct_str = fmt_percent(c_diag_1, precision=4)
    c_diag_2_pct_str = fmt_percent(c_diag_2, precision=4)
```

When $n$ independent Bernoulli trials sampled from the declared fault distribution have zero missed mitigations, the result sets a one-sided upper confidence limit on the miss probability for that distribution. The count is the zero-failure sizing of @sec-evaluation-trial-limits, applied to an injected fault population rather than to runs of a policy. At `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.confidence_pct_str` percent confidence, a `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.p_miss_1_pct_str` percent limit requires `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.n_1_str` zero-miss injections and a `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.p_miss_2_pct_str` percent limit requires `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.n_2_str`. To infer a FIT-weighted hardware coverage (\ref{nbk-verification-hardware-fault-injection-coverage-mean-time} defines the FIT rate and the weights $\lambda_i$), injections must represent the raw-fault weights $\lambda_i$ or use a justified stratified weighting and per-stratum analysis.[^fn-math-zero-failure]

[^fn-math-zero-failure]: **Trial sampling and aging**\index{Zero-failure testing!independence}: The binomial count assumes independent, identically distributed Bernoulli outcomes under the declared injection distribution; it does not require Poisson event arrivals. Repeated heating, wear, or contact changes can break independence and require a state-stratified test design.

The bound applies only when the injection outcomes meet the declared independence and sampling assumptions. Repeated stops heat the drive windings ($I^2R$)\index{Joule heating!fault coupling} and the brake lining, change their resistance and friction, and couple later trials to earlier ones. A campaign run on a dry aisle at room temperature cannot establish a limit for an inspected floor or for the envelope's `{python} RackEndVerification.ambient_lo_str` end.

::: {#nbk-verification-hardware-fault-injection-coverage-mean-time .callout-notebook title="Fault coverage under declared assumptions"}
**Scenario:** Assume component fault rates $\lambda_i$ sum to $\lambda_{\text{raw}}$ = `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_raw_str` FIT, where one FIT is one fault per $10^9$ operating hours. The four illustrative contributions are sensors `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_sensors_str`, compute `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_compute_str`, transceivers and power management `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_power_str`, and gate drivers `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_gate_str` FIT. Let $C_{\text{diag}}$ be the fraction of these faults whose hazardous effect is successfully mitigated, weighted by the applicable fault rates. Then
$$\lambda_{\text{unmitigated}}=\lambda_{\text{raw}}(1-C_{\text{diag}}).$$
A target rate $\lambda_{\text{target}}$ therefore needs $C_{\text{diag}}\ge1-\lambda_{\text{target}}/\lambda_{\text{raw}}$, which is `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.c_diag_1_pct_str` percent for a chosen `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_target_1_str` FIT target and `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.c_diag_2_pct_str` percent for a `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_target_2_str` FIT target.

Zero-miss counts such as `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.n_1_str` injections for a `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.p_miss_1_pct_str` percent limit hold only for a fault population sampled in proportion to its $\lambda_i$ weights. Uniform injections across unequal-rate components estimate a different distribution unless outcomes are weighted and each stratum has adequate evidence. A test must record which mode was injected, whether it was detected, and whether the plant actually reached its allowed state.
:::

Operating hours cannot close what the injections leave open. A zero-event test cannot reach the hazard rates a release claim needs (the exposure wall of @sec-evaluation-trial-limits), so the fault record carries what was never injected as prominently as what passed. It lists every parameter combination omitted because of bench limits, sensor bandwidth, or destructive-test cost, and an untested region therefore cannot reach the safety case of @sec-release as a verified margin.

### Exposure and the population a statistic describes {#sec-verification-exposure-wall}

Operational exposure and deliberate fault injection sample different populations. Under a constant-rate Poisson model, zero occurrences of a specified event over $N$ hours gives the following exposure requirement for a one-sided confidence level $C$:
$$-\lambda N \le \ln(1 - C) \implies N \ge \frac{-\ln(1 - C)}{\lambda}.$$ {#eq-verification-rule-of-three}

At 95 percent confidence $-\ln(1-C) \approx 3$, which is the time-domain form of the rule of three that @sec-evaluation-trial-limits derives for trials (@eq-eval-rule-of-three); that section owns the zero-failure bound. The inverse dependence on the target event rate is the exposure limitation analyzed by @butler1993infeasibility. More fleet hours do not test an omitted fault or establish standards compliance. The event definition, operating conditions, intervention policy, and configuration must match before exposure can support the bound; a changed policy or driver requires an argument for reusing earlier exposure.

### Estimating a rare failure rate by importance sampling {#sec-verification-importance-sampling}

Falsification answers whether a failure exists. Release often needs a different number: how often the failure occurs under the conditions the machine will actually meet. Plain Monte Carlo sampling from those conditions wastes almost every run on a comfortable stop, and a zero-failure campaign bounds the rate only at the scale @sec-evaluation-trial-limits derives. **Importance sampling**\index{Importance sampling!definition} draws the runs from a different distribution that visits the failure region often, then weights each run to undo the bias.

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-rare-event-is
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ IMPORTANCE SAMPLING AND THE CROSS-ENTROPY METHOD ON THE RACK-END OVERSHOOT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-verification-importance-sampling.
# │ Goal: Estimate the probability that an unbudgeted queue delay exhausts the
# │       rack-end reserve, and compare plain Monte Carlo, zero-failure testing,
# │       and importance sampling with a cross-entropy proposal.
# │ Show: failure when the delay exceeds T_latest = 100.8 ms; with an
# │       exponential delay of mean 5 ms, p = 1.8e-9; plain Monte Carlo needs
# │       5.7e10 runs for 10 percent relative error, zero-failure testing 1.7e9;
# │       the cross-entropy proposal (mean 105.8 ms after 4 levels) needs about
# │       2,700 runs, within 0.1 percent of the best exponential proposal.
# │ How: closed forms for an exponential operational delay and an exponential
# │      proposal; the expected (large-sample) cross-entropy iteration.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_zero_failure_sample_size
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_sci, fmt_latency, fmt_percent, check

class RareEventOvershoot:
    """Likelihood-ratio estimate of the rack-end reserve-exhaustion probability."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_exhaust = RackEndVerification.t_spare  # queue delay that spends the reserve (T_latest); category: derived
    d_mean = (
        5 * millisecond
    )  # mean unbudgeted queue delay per stop, exponential; scenario assumption; category: illustrative (a loaded-trial delay histogram would replace it)
    elite_share = 0.1  # cross-entropy elite fraction; category: chosen
    rel_err = 0.1  # target relative standard error of the estimate; category: chosen
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    gamma = float(t_exhaust.to(millisecond).magnitude)
    m0 = float(d_mean.to(millisecond).magnitude)
    lam = 1.0 / m0
    p_true = math.exp(-gamma / m0)  # P(D > T_latest) under the operational model
    n_mc = (1.0 - p_true) / (p_true * rel_err**2)  # plain Monte Carlo runs for the target error
    n_zero = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(1.0 - p_true, confidence=confidence)  # @sec-evaluation-trial-limits
    # Cross-entropy iteration (expected, large-sample form): raise the level to the
    # (1 - elite_share) quantile of the current proposal, refit the proposal mean
    # to the likelihood-weighted elite samples, which for this family is the
    # conditional mean E_p[D | D > level] = level + m0.
    m_k = m0
    levels = []
    while True:
        level = min(gamma, -m_k * math.log(elite_share))
        levels.append(level)
        m_k = level + m0
        if level >= gamma:
            break
    m_ce = m_k
    n_levels = len(levels)
    eta = 1.0 / m_ce

    def _second_moment(eta, lam=lam, gamma=gamma):
        # E_q[w^2 1{D > gamma}] for p = Exp(lam), q = Exp(eta), eta < 2 lam
        return lam**2 / (eta * (2 * lam - eta)) * math.exp(-(2 * lam - eta) * gamma)

    relvar_ce = _second_moment(eta) / p_true**2 - 1.0  # per-sample relative variance
    n_is = relvar_ce / rel_err**2
    p_q_fail = math.exp(-gamma / m_ce)  # share of proposal draws that land in the failure set
    ess_per_draw = eta * (2 * lam - eta) / lam**2  # expected (sum w)^2 / sum w^2 per draw
    n_ess = n_is * ess_per_draw
    # Best exponential proposal: root of t eta^2 - (2 + 2 lam t) eta + 2 lam = 0 below 2 lam
    bq = 2 + 2 * lam * gamma
    eta_opt = (bq - math.sqrt(bq**2 - 8 * lam * gamma)) / (2 * gamma)
    relvar_opt = _second_moment(eta_opt) / p_true**2 - 1.0
    ce_penalty = relvar_ce / relvar_opt - 1.0
    speedup = n_mc / n_is

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(gamma - 100.775) < 5e-3, "Failure threshold is the 100.8 ms spare-exhaustion delay.")
    check(1e-9 < p_true < 1e-8, "Operational failure probability is of order 1e-9.")
    check(n_levels == 4 and abs(m_ce - (gamma + m0)) < 1e-9, "Cross-entropy reaches the threshold in four levels.")
    check(0 <= ce_penalty < 1e-3, "The cross-entropy proposal is within 0.1 percent of the best exponential proposal.")
    check(n_is < 1e4 < n_zero < n_mc, "Importance sampling needs orders of magnitude fewer runs.")
    check(0.3 < p_q_fail < 0.5, "Roughly two in five proposal draws land in the failure set.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    d_mean_str = fmt_latency(d_mean, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    p_true_str = fmt_sci(p_true, precision=1)
    n_mc_str = fmt_sci(n_mc, precision=1)
    n_zero_str = fmt_sci(n_zero, precision=1)
    elite_pct_str = fmt_percent(elite_share, precision=0, style="prose")
    rel_err_pct_str = fmt_percent(rel_err, precision=0, style="prose")
    level_1_str = fmt_latency(levels[0] * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    level_2_str = fmt_latency(levels[1] * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    level_3_str = fmt_latency(levels[2] * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    n_levels_str = fmt_int(n_levels)
    m_ce_str = fmt_latency(m_ce * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    p_q_fail_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_q_fail, precision=1, style="prose")
    relvar_ce_str = fmt(relvar_ce, precision=1)
    n_is_str = fmt_int(math.ceil(n_is), commas=True)
    n_ess_str = fmt_int(round(n_ess), commas=True)
    speedup_str = fmt_sci(speedup, precision=0)
```

Write the operational distribution of the uncertain inputs $x$ as $p(x)$ and the failure event as $F$. Plain Monte Carlo estimates $P_F = \Pr_p(x \in F)$ as the fraction of $N$ draws from $p$ that fail. Importance sampling draws instead from a **proposal distribution** $q(x)$ and weights each draw by the **likelihood ratio** $w(x) = p(x)/q(x)$:
$$\hat{P}_F = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{1}[x_i \in F]\, w(x_i), \qquad x_i \sim q.$$ {#eq-verification-importance-sampling}
The estimator is unbiased whenever $q$ is positive wherever $p$ assigns probability to failure, because the weight exactly undoes the change of distribution [@owen2013monte]. Its variance depends on the choice of $q$. The ideal proposal is $p$ restricted to $F$ and renormalized, which gives every draw the same weight $P_F$ and zero variance; it cannot be used, because building it requires the unknown $P_F$. Practical proposals approximate it.

The **cross-entropy method**\index{Cross-entropy method} [@rubinstein2004cross] finds such an approximation within a chosen family $q_\theta$ by working up through a sequence of easier events. Starting from $q_{\theta_0} = p$, each iteration draws a batch from the current proposal, sets an intermediate level at the $(1-\beta)$ quantile of the failure measure so that a fraction $\beta$ of the batch clears it, and refits $\theta$ by maximizing the likelihood-weighted log-density of those elite draws. The level rises each round until it reaches the true failure threshold, and the final proposal concentrates where failures are most probable under $p$. For an exponential family the refit has a closed form: the new mean is the weighted mean of the elite draws.

Work it on the rack end. The fallacies of @sec-verification-fallacies-pitfalls compute that an unbudgeted queue of $T_{\text{latest}} =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str` spends the whole `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str` reserve at the aisle speed, so a stop overshoots the reserve when its queue delay $D$ exceeds that value. Take, as an illustrative operational model, an exponential delay with mean `{python} RareEventOvershoot.d_mean_str`, the tail of the simplest single-server queue model; a histogram of queue delays from loaded trials on the machine would replace it. Then $P_F = e^{-T_{\text{latest}}/\bar{D}} =$ `{python} RareEventOvershoot.p_true_str` per stop, a value this simple model lets us compute exactly and use to check each estimator.

Plain Monte Carlo needs about $(1-P_F)/(P_F\,r^2)$ runs to reach a relative standard error $r$; for $r$ of `{python} RareEventOvershoot.rel_err_pct_str` that is `{python} RareEventOvershoot.n_mc_str` stops.
